causeGroupMonthlySpendShare.citation: The share of its money a cause group spends each month on its cause. A small volunteer group holds little reserve, so it spends most of what it has each month.
causeGroupMonthlySpendShare.estimatedFrom: Program expense ratios (BBB Wise Giving Alliance; Charity Navigator); spread 0.5 to 1.

causeGroupAdMinimumMinor.citation: The smallest ad buy a local outlet sells, in cents ($100): a group whose month's spending is below it buys nothing and saves toward it. spread.citation: From one short radio spot to a quarter-page in a small daily.

countedGivingShare.estimatedFrom: Applied to the counted adults who share a cause group's concern, as the share of them who give at all.

spread.citation: 49.6% in 2018 against 66.2% in 2000 in the same study.

restingStressBroodingWeight.citation: How much a person who broods dwells on stress, and a person low in brooding is spared it: the shift at the largest recorded brooding trait value (a recorded trait of one tenth of that value moves it a tenth as far). No verified survey table of PSS-10 by personality trait was found; neuroticism-type traits are among the strongest correlates of perceived stress, so the weight lets an extreme trait account for about 10 PSS-10 points (1.5 SD of the norm), since recorded traits cluster near the middle of their range (SD about 0.11 of the maximum).
restingStressBroodingWeight.estimatedFrom: How much a person who broods dwells on stress: the largest shift a recorded brooding trait gives. No verified survey table of PSS-10 by personality trait was found; the size follows the usual finding that neuroticism-type traits are among the strongest correlates of perceived stress, and is set so the modeled spread is a fraction of the norm SD (6.42 points, 0.16).

Before any recorded event a person sits at their own set point, which is 0 on this scale.

appraisalDistressTraitWeight.citation: Bolger, N., & Schilling, E. A. (1991), Personality and the problems of everyday life: The role of neuroticism in exposure and reactivity to daily stressors, Journal of Personality 59(3), 355-386: exposure and reactivity explained over 40% of the distress gap between high- and low-neuroticism people, reactivity twice as much as exposure, so reactivity is about two thirds of that, 0.27 of the gap. Reading the gap as the stressor-driven distress of a low-neuroticism person, the most reactive person (brooding and concern for distress at the top of the scale) responds about 1 + 2/3 times as strongly as the least; with the two appraisal traits multiplying, a trait at 2 levels reads 2/3 of the way up the trait scale of 3, so a weight of 0.255 each moves it 0.17 and gives (1.17 x 1.17) / (1 - 0.17) = 1.65. This weight is for concern for distress.

spread.citation: Ratio of most to least reactive 1.3 to 2.1 across a reactivity share of 0.2 to 0.4 of the gap.

appraisalDistressTraitWeight.estimatedFrom: The paper reports shares of the distress gap, not a per-trait response slope (its tables were not retrieved); the reading of the gap as the low-neuroticism stressor response is an assumption.

(1991), Personality and the problems of everyday life: The role of neuroticism in exposure and reactivity to daily stressors, Journal of Personality 59(3), 355-386: exposure and reactivity explained over 40% of the distress gap between high- and low-neuroticism people, reactivity twice as much as exposure, so reactivity is about two thirds of that, 0.27 of the gap. Reading the gap as the stressor-driven distress of a low-neuroticism person, the most reactive person (brooding and concern for distress at the top of the scale) responds about 1 + 2/3 times as strongly as the least; with the two appraisal traits multiplying, a trait at 2 levels reads 2/3 of the way up the trait scale of 3, so a weight of 0.255 each moves it 0.17 and gives (1.17 x 1.17) / (1 - 0.17) = 1.65. This weight is for brooding.

spread.citation: Ratio of most to least reactive 1.3 to 2.1 across a reactivity share of 0.2 to 0.4 of the gap.

appraisalBroodingTraitWeight.estimatedFrom: The paper reports shares of the distress gap, not a per-trait response slope (its tables were not retrieved); the reading of the gap as the low-neuroticism stressor response is an assumption.

closenessHoursAtHalf.citation: Hours of time together at which closeness reaches half of full closeness; closeness is hours / (hours + this value), so it grows toward full closeness and never reaches it.

spread.citation: Hall (2019), How many hours does it take to make a friend?, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships 36(4): 80 to 100 hours to become a friend, combined across both studies; roughly 50 hours to a casual friend and more than 200 to a close friend.

openingPeerTieHours.citation: Hours of time together two people have at the opening when the records say they shared a school class or a workgroup in the town. Hall (2019), How many hours does it take to make a friend?, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships 36(4): about 50 hours of time together to move from acquaintance to casual friend (the same study that sets closenessHoursAtHalf).
openingPeerTieHours.estimatedFrom: Hall's roughly 50 hours to a casual friend, used as the estimated initial time together for every recorded school classmate and coworker. Shared hours and stint lengths are not measured per pair; the tie fades by the closeness half-life from the recorded day the shared context began, including for a current coworker. This is the registered opening approximation, not an observed duration for each pair.

spread.citation: Hall (2019): 40 to 60 hours to a casual friend, 80 to 100 to a friend.

closenessKinHalfLifeDays.citation: Half-life of time together between relatives without contact, 36 months, as the P15 package and the P13 director use it. Roberts and Dunbar (2015) report kin closeness holding steady while friends' fell, but give no half-life. Calibration check: Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014), Social Networks 37, 65-80 (Dutch panel, 1,007 adults aged 18-65, 604 re-interviewed seven years later): 48% of the discussion partners and practical helpers named at the start were still in the network seven years later, and 30% held the same position (figures as reported in the Utrecht University release of May 27, 2009, ScienceDaily 090527111907; the 2014 article is paywalled and no kin/non-kin split was found in the sources read). The game's share of ties still above their opening closeness after seven years is compared with it in a seven-year run.

spread.reason: No study reports a half-life for closeness without contact; Roberts and Dunbar (2015) report direction only (kin b = 0.27, friends b = -0.62 over 18 months).

closenessOtherHalfLifeDays.citation: Half-life of time together between people who are not relatives without contact, 18 months, as the P15 package and the P13 director use it. Calibration check: Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014), Social Networks 37, 65-80 (Dutch panel, 1,007 adults aged 18-65, 604 re-interviewed seven years later): 48% of the discussion partners and practical helpers named at the start were still in the network seven years later, and 30% held the same position (figures as reported in the Utrecht University release of May 27, 2009, ScienceDaily 090527111907; the 2014 article is paywalled and no kin/non-kin split was found in the sources read). The game's share of ties still above their opening closeness after seven years is compared with it in a seven-year run.

spread.reason: No study reports a half-life for closeness without contact; Roberts and Dunbar (2015) report that friendships decline faster than kinship.

householdFamilyMinutesPerDay.citation: Kannan and Veazie (2022), SSM Population Health 21:101331, American Time Use Survey 2019: average minutes per day in the presence of household family members, respondents 15 and older.

circleRetentionShareOverSpan.citation: Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014), Social Networks 37, 65-80, Dutch panel of 1,007 adults aged 18-65, 604 re-interviewed seven years later: "Only 48 percent were still part of the network" (discussion partners and practical helpers; Utrecht University release of May 27, 2009, https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/05/090527111907.htm, fetched 2026-10-24; data/research/people/mollenhorst-2014-network-turnover.json). A secondary report of the study; the article's tables were not readable. It checks totals across many circles and never decides one tie's fate.

spread.unit: share of the starting circle still in it after the span
spread.citation: 95% binomial interval of 0.48 among the 604 re-interviewed (1.96 * sqrt(0.48 * 0.52 / 604) = 0.04); sampling error only (data/research/people/mollenhorst-2014-network-turnover.json).

circleRetentionSpanYears.citation: Span over which circleRetentionShareOverSpan was measured: the Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014) panel re-interviewed respondents seven years after the first wave (same release and research file).

spread.reason: The study has one fixed re-interview span; no other span was measured.

householdOtherMinutesPerDay.citation: Minutes per day a housemate who is not family spends in another housemate's presence; ATUS 2019 reports 43 minutes per day with all 'others' (roommates, neighbors, acquaintances, coworkers and clients) together, used here as the housemate figure.

spread.reason: ATUS does not separate roommates from neighbors, acquaintances, coworkers and clients.

spread.reason: Hall (2019) reports that work and school hours count less, not by how much.

farKinContactShare.citation: Visits to a relative living outside the household's county, as a share of visits to one in the same county. Pew Research Center, 'As Family Forms Change, Bonds Remain Strong' (survey 2005, released 2006), table 'Living Closer to Parents Means More Contact' (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2010/10/FamilyBonds.pdf): 56% of adults with a parent in the same town see or talk to them every day, against 22% with a parent out of town (data/research/core/pew-2006-family-contact.json, checked by scripts/research/core-parameters-check.ts).
farKinContactShare.estimatedFrom: Ratio of the two daily-contact shares, 22 / 56 = 0.39, applied to visits to any relative outside the county. Pew counts calls with visits and compares towns, not counties or travel times; the CTO accepted it until relatives carry a place (October 10, 2026). The measured figure that would make it SOURCED is contact by travel time between the two places, which no fetched U.S. page gives.

spread.unit: ratio of contact with a relative out of town to one in town
spread.citation: Pew Research Center 2006, same table: the daily-contact ratio (22 / 56 = 0.39) to the ratio of contacts a year over the whole distribution (111.4 / 225.2 = 0.49, coding daily 365, weekly 52, monthly 12, several times a year 4, yearly 1); data/research/core/pew-2006-family-contact.json.

causeHolderWeeklyContacts.citation: How many of their ties a person with a cause weighs contacting in a week (owner decision SG-PEOPLE-cause-holder-weekly-contacts). Studies of personal networks find layers of about 5 people in closest weekly touch and about 12 to 15 contacted at least monthly (the 'sympathy group'; Dunbar and colleagues' network-layer studies); the value is the upper layer, so the shortlist binds only for people whose cause has tied them to many more.

spread.citation: From the closest weekly layer to the monthly 'sympathy group' of personal-network studies; to be sourced from pages fetched by research before it leaves TUNABLE.

focusDailyContactDays.citation: How long after the player last had contact with someone in focus (outside the player's family and household) that person keeps choosing daily; after it they choose at their tier's cadence until the two meet again. The contact date is read from the indexed tie. A scheduling cadence, like the tiers' own, not a behavior. Measured Oct 25 in Bedford, Wyoming (seed 9a4dd331ace7) with a prototype: the third year fell from 2.05 to 1.28 times the first.

spread.citation: From two weeks, about the gap between a weekly group's meetings missed twice, to a season; checked against the year-three speed band (speed:year).

extendedKinVisitShare.citation: Visits to one grandparent, grandchild, aunt, uncle, niece, nephew or a child's other parent, as a share of the GSS frequency of a social evening with any relative.

spread.reason: The GSS asks about relatives as a group; no source gives visits per extended relative.

tieMissingWeightPerHour.citation: Pull toward contacting a person for each hour of time together the tie has lost since the last contact. Chosen in a sweep of a 600-resident generated Stanwood, Washington town (56 days, seed p15-opening-kin), where higher values added little contact and crowded out other acts. Checked in a 10,001-resident Sacramento town over 91 days (seed p10-drives-proof-2026-10-09): adults made 47.4 visits a year to relatives outside their home, about 91 hours against 170 in ATUS 2019 (28 minutes a day, Kannan and Veazie 2022), and visited each parent 2.5 times as often as each sibling against 1.37 in the GSS. One discretionary act per activation caps the total.

spread.reason: No source measures how strongly a fading tie pulls a person to make contact.

deepPastMiddleSchoolOffsetYears.citation: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey October 2024 School Enrollment, Table 2, Single Grade of Enrollment by single year of age (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/tables/school-enrollment/2024/2024-cps/enroll02_2024_1.xlsx), in data/research/core/cps-2024-grade-by-age.json and checked by scripts/research/deep-past-check.ts: the modal grade (the Census Bureau's "year of school in which the largest proportion of students of a given age is enrolled") of 5-year-olds is kindergarten (2,540 thousand) and of 11-year-olds grade 6 (2,613 thousand).
deepPastMiddleSchoolOffsetYears.estimatedFrom: Converted from a cross-sectional enrollment table, not a measured duration. The value is the modal age of grade 6 minus the modal age of kindergarten (11 - 5 = 6 years). The spread's high end is the 6 grades divided by the mean pace of enrolled children, the rise in mean grade per year of age from age 6 to age 11 (0.98 grades a year), which gives 6.13 years. Limit: Table 2 counts children by age and grade in one October, so it does not time any child's entry into a grade; the October age cutoff, early or late starts and held-back children are mixed into the modal ages, and the high end counts children held back, whom the deep past does not hold back. The figure becomes SOURCED when a source that follows children from kindergarten entry times the years to grade 6.

spread.unit: years from kindergarten entry to grade 6 entry
spread.citation: Same table: on-time progression takes 6 years; at the mean pace of enrolled children (mean grade 0.84 at age 6 and 5.73 at age 11, 0.98 grades a year) it takes 6.13.

workSleepReserveHours.citation: BLS American Time Use Survey 2025, Table 8B (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/atus.t08b.htm), employed adults 18 and over, annual averages: sleeping 8.83 hours per diary day with no household child under 18, 8.56 with one. Recorded in data/research/core/atus-2025-sleep.json, checked by scripts/research/core-parameters-check.ts.

spread.citation: BLS ATUS 2025 Table 8B, employed adults: with a household child under 18 (8.56) to with none (8.83).

workSleepReserveHours.estimatedFrom: The midpoint of the two employed-adult figures in Table 8B, because the table gives no total for employed adults and the share of employed adults with a child at home is not read here. It replaces the all-adults mean of 9.03, which includes people who do not work. One reserve serves every person and every day; the figure that would make it SOURCED is each person's own ATUS group (age, employed or not, a child at home), read per person.

restDayHours.citation: BLS American Time Use Survey 2025, Table 3: leisure and sports, 5.16 hours per day for people 15 and over (src/core2/data/time-use-reference.json).
restDayHours.estimatedFrom: The rest act stands for the day's leisure: the free-time planner (free-block.ts) takes at most one act per need per day, so one rest act is the whole day's leisure and takes the ATUS daily leisure and sports time, averaged over everyone 15 and over (CTO, October 10, 2026: rest gets a real leisure length so it competes for the evening). Measured Oct 19: shortening it to one sitting cuts the leisure hours per day almost in proportion, because a person still rests once a day (docs/pool/items/core-recovery-hours-per-offer.md). ATUS leisure ranges from 3.89 hours (35 to 44) to 7.39 (75 and over); one value serves every age here.

businessIncomeElasticity.citation: Inherited old town-finances sales proxy. Moretti Local Multipliers, https://eml.berkeley.edu/~moretti/multipliers.pdf, Table 1 reports employment-to-employment elasticity; it does not report sales-to-all-town-income elasticity. This coefficient is uncalibrated.

spread.reason: Employment elasticity uncertainty is not a bound for this sales response coefficient. Matched sales/income data and identification are missing.

businessIncomeHalfLifeDays.citation: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics, state unemployment-rate gaps 2000–2025: half-life implied by their AR(1) persistence, median across the 50 states (data/research/regional/roadmap-r1-gap-persistence.json, research roadmap R1).

spread.citation: P10 and P90 across the 50 states.

businessIncomeHalfLifeDays.estimatedFrom: How fast a town's sales follow a change in its residents' income is read from how fast local labor-market gaps close; the median state's half-life is 785 days.

businessCrowdingResponse.citation: Nakamura and Steinsson (2008), 'Five Facts about Prices,' Quarterly Journal of Economics 123(4), Table I (https://business.columbia.edu/sites/default/files-efs/pubfiles/3556/fivefacts.pdf): median monthly frequency of regular price change 8.7-11.9%.

spread.unit: monthly log price change per unit of excess demand
spread.citation: f from 0.087 to 0.119 (Nakamura and Steinsson 2008) over e from 3 (rival sellers, Broda and Weinstein 2006) to 0.5 (market demand).

businessCrowdingResponse.estimatedFrom: Derived: a firm closes about the monthly change frequency f of its price gap each month, and clearing excess demand x takes a price move of x over the demand elasticity e it faces, so the response is about f/e; f = 0.10 and e = 1 give 0.1.

businessPriceStepMaximum.citation: A per-review cap on the price move from demand pressure. Nakamura and Steinsson (2008), 'Five Facts about Prices,' QJE 123(4): the median absolute size of a regular consumer price change is 8.5% (6.1% to 14.2% by major group), made about once every 8 to 11 months; a monthly cap of 5% keeps a monthly review's move below one typical change.

spread.citation: Nakamura and Steinsson (2008): per-change sizes 6.1%-14.2% by major group; the cap is checked from 0.05 up to that range.

businessRivalPriceElasticity.citation: Broda and Weinstein (2006), 'Globalization and the Gains from Variety,' Quarterly Journal of Economics 121(2), Table 4 (FRBNY Staff Report 180, https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/staff_reports/sr180.html): median elasticity of substitution between varieties, 1990-2001, 2.7 at SITC-5.

spread.unit: elasticity of substitution between rival sellers
spread.citation: Broda and Weinstein (2006), SITC-5 10th and 90th percentiles, 1990-2001.

businessRivalPriceElasticity.estimatedFrom: US import varieties by source country, used for rival local sellers of one kind; close local substitutes are likely more elastic than the median.

salesTaxPassThrough.citation: Poterba, 'Retail Price Reactions to Changes in State and Local Sales Taxes', National Tax Journal 49(2), 1996, pp. 165-176, abstract: 'retail prices rise by approximately the amount of the sales tax', and the paper finds it 'never possible to reject the null hypothesis that prices rise point-for-point with changes in the retail sales tax'; Besley and Rosen, National Tax Journal 52(2), 1999 (NBER Working Paper 6667): 'For some commodities, the after-tax price increases by exactly the amount of the tax.' Read by the business price review (src/core2/finance-state.ts): a change in what a seller keeps of each dollar of its tax-inclusive sales moves its tax-inclusive price by this many times that change, so at one the price before tax holds still (the outcome web's sales-tax-to-prices row).

spread.unit: change in the tax-inclusive price per unit change in the tax
spread.citation: From Poterba's 1925-39 estimate (0.62) and Gracner et al. (2022), about 60% pass-through of taxes on energy-dense food in Mexico 2012-2016, to Zhao, Barrett, Zheng and Kaiser, 'The Incidence of Grocery Taxes in U.S. Food and Factor Markets' (Cornell University, August 2025 revision; https://barrett.dyson.cornell.edu/files/papers/Incidence_of_Grocery_Taxes_AJAE_Revision_R2.pdf): 'a grocery tax that generates $1 in grocery tax revenue leads to a $1.44 rise in tax-inclusive consumer food prices.'

businessRepaymentShare.citation: Old town-finances repays debt from half of positive cash; authored liquidity/repayment policy, not a sourced behavior rule.

spread.reason: Requires actual debt-contract and firm cash/repayment observations; no behavior coefficient bounds measured.

businessOwnPriceElasticity.citation: Old town-finances DEFAULT_PRICE_ELASTICITY is explicitly PLACEHOLDER; not a common measured elasticity for every industry.

spread.reason: Sector-specific price/quantity and spending data are required; no matched coefficient bounds established.

businessRestaurantOwnPriceElasticity.citation: Old town-finances references Andreyeva, Long and Brownell, AJPH 2010, food-away-from-home aggregate demand elasticity. Carrying that magnitude into this generated market/price projection is an uncalibrated crosswalk, not a measured firm coefficient.

spread.reason: The food-away-from-home category/study spread has not been reconstructed and does not identify this town-market price coefficient. Require matching source quantities and market observations.

financeAct365FixedDays.citation: ISDA day-count definitions: Actual/365 Fixed divides actual elapsed days by 365. Applying that convention to prototype loan contracts is an openly recorded settlement-policy assumption; an explicit facility can bind a different registered day-count denominator.

openingFinancePeriodMonths.citation: Prototype monthly standing purchase-budget aggregation; no source identifies this settlement cadence or its first-next-month due phase.

spread.reason: No matched household/firm purchase timing distribution or identified cadence interval; monthly aggregation is an authored prototype policy.

financeObservableFullTimeHours.citation: BLS CPS 2019 annual averages, Table 8, employed persons by usual full- or part-time status at all jobs: full time is 35 hours or more per week. https://www.bls.gov/cps/aa2019/cpsaat08.htm . Definition-only observation boundary; not an employment probability, individual behavior threshold, coefficient, observed hours spread, or calibration pass. Archived source: src/core2/receipts/work-hours-v5-source-audit/evidence.json, BLS-CPS-2019-T8.

openingRetirementCareerStartAgeYears.citation: Canonical town-employment.ts WORKING_AGE_MIN=18 and current P8 adulthood convention, used only as a bounded fictional covered-career start prior; not observed past employment.
openingRetirementCareerStartAgeYears.estimatedFrom: Explicit opening-generation prior. No claim of observed individual history, 2021 legal entitlement or parameter-specific empirical bound.

openingRetirementSchoolContextYears.citation: Existing shared school-calendar common high-school grades 9–12. Four modeled years bound a possible post-cohort career start; a cohort record does not grant graduation or employment.
openingRetirementSchoolContextYears.estimatedFrom: Explicit opening-generation prior. No claim of observed individual history, 2021 legal entitlement or parameter-specific empirical bound.

openingRetirementClaimAgeYears.citation: Calibration target, no longer the claim age itself: SSA's average age at entitlement for claims made 2000–2020 was 63.4–65.0 (Annual Statistical Supplement 2021, Table 6.B5.1). The claim is a decision inside the law (src/core2/retirement-claim.ts).
openingRetirementClaimAgeYears.estimatedFrom: The opening retiree stock claimed over about 1985–2020, when the average award age was 63.4–65.0; awards at full retirement age include disability conversions the generator doesn't model.

spread.citation: SSA Table 6.B5 (2022) distribution of award ages.

openingRetirementClaimTraitPullYears.citation: SSA Annual Statistical Supplement 2022, Table 6.B5: claim ages spread from 62 (about 25% in 2021) to 70 and later (about 8%); one unit of patience (mean of deliberation, reliability and less risk) moves a claim about a year and a half.
openingRetirementClaimTraitPullYears.estimatedFrom: Explicit opening-generation prior. No claim of observed individual history, 2021 legal entitlement or parameter-specific empirical bound.

spread.reason: No empirical individual dispersion or coefficient interval identified. Contextual person variation is not the source mean standard error.

openingRetirementClaimTraitPullYears.checkedAgainst: Measured once over three generated openings (seeds claim-a/b/c, 3,694 retirees): mean claim age 64.08 (SSA 63.4–65.0), 20% at 62 (SSA 2021 about 25%); claiming at 70 (SSA about 8%) is not reached yet.

openingRetirementCoveredFraction.citation: SSA, Social Security Bulletin 65(1), 'Outcome Indicators' (https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/ssb/v65n1/v65n1p70.html): share of quarters with covered earnings from age 22 to the year before first claiming, men retiring in 2002 0.84, women 0.66. CRS R47330 (SSA estimates for 1950–1959 cohorts): 62% of workers surviving to 67 have 35 or more covered years between 22 and 67.
openingRetirementCoveredFraction.estimatedFrom: The source counts quarters from age 22; the game's adults start at 18 (openingRetirementCareerStartAgeYears), so each share is turned into covered years over the claim age less 22 and divided by the years from 18: 0.75 (the men's and women's shares averaged) times (64.08 - 22) / (64.08 - 18) = 0.685, using the opening's measured mean claim age of 64.08. One value for everyone until people's own work histories carry it.

spread.unit: share of adult years (from 18) with covered earnings
spread.citation: SSA Bulletin 65(1): women 0.66 and men 0.84 from age 22, each times (64.08 - 22) / (64.08 - 18).

openingRetirementCoveredTraitPull.citation: Authored signed reliability-context contribution to the fictional covered-career fraction, smoothly bounded to its possible span; not an empirically measured work history effect.
openingRetirementCoveredTraitPull.estimatedFrom: Explicit opening-generation prior. No claim of observed individual history, 2021 legal entitlement or parameter-specific empirical bound.

spread.reason: No empirical individual dispersion or coefficient interval identified. Contextual person variation is not the source mean standard error.

openingRetirementMinimumCoveredMonths.citation: Social Security Act §214(a), 42 U.S.C. 414(a): fully insured status needs 40 quarters of coverage (about 10 years) for workers born after 1928; SSA Publication 05-10072, How You Earn Credits.
openingRetirementMinimumCoveredMonths.estimatedFrom: 40 quarters = 120 months. Real credits come from earnings (up to 4 a year), so modeled covered months are an analog of the legal threshold.

openingRetirementBenefitMonthlyMinor.citation: Official SSA 2021 COLA factsheet, estimated average monthly Social Security benefits payable in January 2021, All Retired Workers after 1.3% COLA = $1,543. https://www.ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2021.html ; linked by October 13, 2020 announcement. Converted to 154300 USD minor units as a source-reported average estimate, not measured individual awards, net bank receipts, eligibility or individual dispersion.
openingRetirementBenefitMonthlyMinor.estimatedFrom: SSA estimated January 2021 retired-worker mean; existing fictional covered-career factor and person variation are uncalibrated. No average-mean sampling interval or amount-distribution crosswalk identified.

openingRetirementBenefitReferenceCovered.citation: Social Security Act §215(b)(2), 42 U.S.C. 415(b)(2): the average indexed monthly earnings use the highest 35 computation years for workers born 1929 or later; SSA Publication 05-10070, Your Retirement Benefit: How It's Figured.
openingRetirementBenefitReferenceCovered.estimatedFrom: 35 years × 12 = 420 months; dividing covered months by 420 approximates the zero-year penalty, not the earnings level or the bend points.

openingRetirementBenefitFactorMinimum.citation: SSA, Annual Statistical Supplement 2021, Table 5.B6 (retired workers by monthly benefit, December 2020; 46,329,595 workers, average $1,544.15), https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/statcomps/supplement/2021/5b.html: the 5th percentile benefit, computed from the published bins, is 0.33 of the mean.

openingRetirementBenefitFactorMaximum.citation: SSA, Annual Statistical Supplement 2021, Table 5.B6 (December 2020), https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/statcomps/supplement/2021/5b.html: the 95th percentile benefit, computed from the published bins, is 1.88 times the mean.

openingRetirementPeriodMonths.citation: Sourced monthly benefit cadence only. The first bill on the first day of the next month and later fixed-day successors in opening-income.ts remain an explicitly ESTIMATED calendar prior. They do not implement 20 CFR 404.1807 insured-worker cycling, exceptions or holiday/early-payment rules; see src/core2/data/research/retirement-opening-2021.json observations.ssaPaymentDayRule2020.

openingRetirementFundingPublicAnnualOutl.citation: Evidence only: SSA 2021 Trustees Report Table III.A1 reports $952,362 million OASI net benefit payments for calendar 2020, published August 31, 2021; src/core2/data/research/retirement-opening-2021.json observations.oasiNetBenefitPayments2020. Rounded-in-millions annual flow with scheduled-benefit-year adjustment, not a stock, 2021 actor knowledge, allocation, cap or end. The retirement funding producer does not read this parameter.

openingCustomerPublicCleaningBudgetShare.citation: Cleaning share of local general-public-buildings spending = cleaning's share of an office building's operating cost times the current-operations share of that spending. BOMA International, Experience Exchange Report, 2012 data (reported by Building Design+Construction, Nov. 6, 2013): total operating expenses $7.86 per square foot, cleaning $1.44 (derived from '$0.06 (4.0 percent) less'); https://bdcnetwork.com/energy-efficiency-measures-paying-commercial-building-owners-says-boma-study?page=11. U.S. Census Bureau, 2022 Census of Governments: Finance, 22statetypepu.txt, local E31 $9,275,602 thousand of E31+F31 $13,733,818 thousand; https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/gov-finances/tables/2022/2022_Individual_Unit_File.zip. Research files data/research/core/building-operating-cost-janitorial-share.json and data/research/core/census-2022-local-public-buildings-by-government-type.json; checked by scripts/research/check-opening-customer-priors.ts.
openingCustomerPublicCleaningBudgetShare.estimatedFrom: 0.183 (BOMA 2012 cleaning / total operating expenses) x 0.6754 (Census 2022 local general-public-buildings current operations / current operations plus construction) = 0.124. Office-building benchmarks stand in for public buildings; the town's public employers carry no custodian role (src/core2/town-workplaces.ts), so the whole cleaning share is bought from building-services firms.

spread.citation: Low: BOMA 2012 cleaning share 0.183 x the 10th-percentile state current-operations share 0.4988; high: IFMA 2000 median janitorial share 0.193 ($1.08 of $5.59 per square foot, https://www.fmlink.com/?p=13268) x the 90th-percentile state share 0.9294 (Census 2022, 51 states and D.C.).

openingCustomerLocalAuthorityBudgetCover.citation: U.S. Census Bureau, 2022 Census of Governments: Finance, 22statetypepu.txt: county, municipal and township governments make all local general-public-buildings spending (current operations 9,275,602 thousand; special and school districts 0), counties 4,625,728 thousand (0.4987); https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/gov-finances/tables/2022/2022_Individual_Unit_File.zip. Census 2025 Government Units listing (src/core2/reference/government-units.ts): 19,482 of the 32,508 playable places have a municipal or township government. Research file data/research/core/census-2022-local-public-buildings-by-government-type.json; checked by scripts/research/check-opening-customer-priors.ts.
openingCustomerLocalAuthorityBudgetCover.estimatedFrom: The buyers are the place's own general-purpose government and its county. Where both buy, they represent all of the spending (1.0); where the county is the only buyer (a census-designated place) it represents the county share 0.4987. Weighted by the playable places: 0.5993 x 1 + 0.4007 x 0.4987 = 0.8. One national value until the opening reads each place's buyer types against its state's shares (per-state table in the research file).

spread.citation: Low: the 10th-percentile county share among the 48 states with county governments (0.243), a county-only buyer; high: 1.0, the county and the place's own government together (Census 2022 Census of Governments: Finance, 22statetypepu.txt).

openingEmployerCashBufferTailSpan.citation: JPMorgan Chase Institute, Cash Is King: Flows, Balances, and Buffer Days, September 2016, Figure 5 (distribution of cash buffer days, printed page 14); https://www.jpmorganchase.com/content/dam/jpmc/jpmorgan-chase-and-co/institute/pdf/jpmc-institute-small-business-report.pdf; original PDF SHA256 e4ddf6731fd32b239ec9d0afd308791c3b0155fe9f8396b4d80a8221e268eef7. Lower-tail cross-check: U.S. Census Bureau, Small Business Pulse Survey, April 11 to 17, 2022, https://portal.census.gov/pulse/data/downloads/72/national_sector_11Apr22_17Apr22.xlsx (data/research/core/census-sbps-cash-on-hand-2022.json).
openingEmployerCashBufferTailSpan.estimatedFrom: Figure 5's drawn density of cash buffer days, integrated from its vector outline: the three quartile regions it draws hold 26.5, 24.2 and 24.3 percent of the area up to 62 days, and 10.1 percent of firms lie between the 75th percentile (62 days) and 100 days, so 14.9 percent hold more than 100. The opening quantile curve's straight top segment puts 0.25 x (100 - 62) / (high - 62) of firms in that band, so high = 156 days and the tail span is (156 - 62) / (62 - 27) = 2.69, rounded to 2.7. At this span every industry's lowest buffer reaches zero days, as the outline's nonzero density at 0 days and the pulse survey's 3.6 percent of employer firms with no cash (10.7 percent with 7 days or less, against 10.6 in Figure 5) show. One all-industries outline sets the span for all thirteen industry curves; straight tail segments, uniform startup ranks and the generated-employer cash-debit crosswalk remain assumptions.

spread.unit: tail span: quartile-to-median intervals from the 75th percentile to the curve's top endpoint (and from the 25th down to its bottom)
spread.citation: Same Figure 5 outline (data/research/core/jpmci-cash-buffer-days-2016.json), taking each of its three drawn quartile regions in turn as the 25 percent unit (scripts/research/opening-capital-tail-span.ts); the range of the figure's own reading, not a sampling interval.

kinMoveAwayShare.citation: Share of moves out of the county (ACS 2024 B07401, by state and age) that take a person away from their family, rather than to a nearby county or back home. One value cannot reach both PSID 2013 figures (74.8% nearest parent or grown child within 30 miles, 35.5% all of them). In a generated Sacramento town of 3,000 (seed p10-drives-proof-2026-10-09, with later-life re-aging), 0.3 gives 71.1% and 42.4%, and 0.35 gives 67.1% and 37.5%; 0.35 has the smaller combined miss.

spread.reason: No source splits moves out of the county into moves away from family and short or return moves; PSID reports only the resulting distances (74.8% have the nearest parent or grown child within 30 miles, 35.5% all of them).

spouseAgeGapOpenRowYears.citation: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey 2023 Annual Social and Economic Supplement public use file (asecpub23csv.zip, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/cps/datasets/2023/march/asecpub23csv.zip), counted in data/research/core/cps-asec-2023-partner-age-gap.json and checked by scripts/research/deep-past-check.ts: the 746 thousand married couples in Table FG3's two open rows (20 or more years apart) are on average 27.34 years apart (husband older 26.41, wife older 30.27); the counts reproduce Table FG3 row for row.
spouseAgeGapOpenRowYears.estimatedFrom: The engine spreads each open row evenly over this many whole years from 20; an even spread over w years has a mean gap of 20 + (w - 1) / 2, so the pooled mean of 27.34 years gives w = 15.69, rounded to 16. Before, five years (20 to 24) left out the 43% of husband-older and 62% of wife-older open-row couples who are 25 or more years apart. Reading the single-year tail itself in place of an even spread is the partnership builder's change.

spread.unit: whole years an open age-gap row is spread over
spread.citation: CPS 2023 ASEC public use file, data/research/core/cps-asec-2023-partner-age-gap.json: the even width matching each open row's own mean gap, 13.82 years where the husband is 20 or more years older and 21.55 where the wife is.

openingCoworkerGroupSize.citation: Typical generated workgroup of residents at one employer (groups are drawn person by person, so sizes vary around it) whose members know each other by name; prototype choice pending a US source on how many coworkers people know. griefResilientShare.citation: Bonanno, Wortman, Lehman et al. (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, Results: of 205 widowed adults followed at 6 and 18 months, 94 (45.9%) showed the resilient pattern.
griefResilientShare.estimatedFrom: Taken as the share whose grief has fallen to little by 6 months after a death. The study measured widowed adults aged about 72; the game applies it to every relative's loss (owner ruling, October 10, 2026).

griefChronicShare.citation: Bonanno, Wortman, Lehman et al. (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, Results: of 205 widowed adults followed at 6 and 18 months, 32 (15.6%) showed chronic grief.
griefChronicShare.estimatedFrom: Taken as the share whose grief is still above little at 18 months. The 7.8% with chronic depression began depressed before the loss and are not counted here.

griefEarlyCheckMonths.citation: Bonanno, Wortman, Lehman et al. (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, Results: of 205 widowed adults followed at 6 and 18 months: the first follow-up, 6 months after the loss.

griefLateCheckMonths.citation: Bonanno, Wortman, Lehman et al. (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, Results: of 205 widowed adults followed at 6 and 18 months: the second follow-up, 18 months after the loss.

griefLittleFraction.citation: Share of the grief at a death that counts as little grief when the resilience spread is solved from Bonanno et al. (2002); the study classified people by depression and grief scores, not by a share of starting grief, so this is a modeling choice.

spread.reason: No empirical range identified; Bonanno et al. (2002) classify grief patterns by scores, not by this quantity.

griefPullWeight.citation: Pull of grief toward rest and contact with family, per unit of grief; no direct source.

griefHoldWeight.citation: Hold of grief on organizing, per unit of grief (negative: grief makes organizing less attractive); no direct source. CTO REVIEW 11: grief first pulls toward withdrawal and family.

spread.reason: No empirical range identified; Bonanno et al. (2002) classify grief patterns by scores, not by this quantity.

schoolFinalGrade.citation: U.S. public schools end with grade 12 (the existing game school-calendar.ts: grades 9-12 in high school).

householdChildAgeYears.citation: BLS American Time Use Survey: household children are those under 18 (ATUS glossary, 'household children'); https://www.bls.gov/tus/glossary.htm

unmodeledLeisureValuePerHour.citation: Score an hour of the leisure the game does not model is worth; an act added to a free block after the activation's pick must score above its hours times this. Calibrated so visits fall on the ATUS 2025 share of people who socialize or communicate on a given day (30.4%, Table 1); no direct source for the value itself. Calibrated on two generated towns of 1,000 residents over 28 days (seeds p15-visit-a and -b: Albertville, Alabama; Kennedale, Texas): 0.4 gave 33.9% and 0.5 gave 28.6% of adult-days with a visit. Band (Oct 23, 2026): ATUS 2025 Table 1, socializing and communicating, 30.4% of people 15 and over on an average day (men 28.2%, women 32.5%), in data/research/core/atus-2025-socializing.json; scripts/research/core-year.ts reports the town's share of adult-days with a visit against it and scripts/research/check-core-research.ts checks the file.

spread.reason: No published effect converts to the value of an hour in these score units (ATUS gives time and shares of people, not a score); the ATUS share is an outcome band the year run reports against, not a bound on this value.
