driveStatusHalfLifeDays.citation: Half-life of a drive's pull without new events or acts. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No measured persistence of status ambition after a setback has been identified.

driveCallingHalfLifeDays.citation: Half-life of a drive's pull without new events or acts. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No measured persistence of vocational callings after a formative event has been identified.

driveActReinforcement.citation: Share of a drive's unfilled strength that each act on it fills (commitment and consistency), so repeated acts level off below the ceiling of one. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: Commitment-consistency studies report behavior shifts, not a strength unit on this scale.

perceptionTraitWeight.citation: Weight of each relevant trait on how heavily a perception channel counts. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No instrument-matched bound links these trait scores to event salience.

perceptionClosenessWeight.citation: Extra attention per unit of recorded relationship level with the event's subject. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No measured bound in this relationship unit has been identified.

perceptionRoleSubject.citation: Attention weight when the event happened to the person. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: Role weights are relative prototype assumptions with no measured bounds.

perceptionRoleFamily.citation: Attention weight when the event happened to a recorded relative. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: Role weights are relative prototype assumptions with no measured bounds.

perceptionRoleHousehold.citation: Attention weight when the event happened to a household member who is not recorded family. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: Role weights are relative prototype assumptions with no measured bounds.

perceptionRoleAcquaintance.citation: Attention weight when the event happened to someone the person knows. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: Role weights are relative prototype assumptions with no measured bounds.

perceptionRoleWitness.citation: Attention weight for a person who witnessed or was told of an event without another recorded tie. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: Role weights are relative prototype assumptions with no measured bounds.

driveShareHours.citation: Time a person spends telling someone about their cause. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No ATUS category isolates conversations about a cause.

causeShareImpulseScale.citation: Stress and mood impulse a listener receives per unit of the teller's drive strength. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No measured bound for secondhand distress on this scale has been identified.

donateHours.citation: Time spent making one donation. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No ATUS category isolates making a donation.

donationShareOfSpare.citation: The share of a person's cash above their buffer (moneyBufferDays of living cost) they give in one gift to a cause they hold at full strength; a weaker hold gives proportionally less. Checked against what U.S. households give to causes like these: Giving USA 2024 reports $374.40 billion of individual giving in 2023, about 16% of all giving going to public-society benefit and environment and animal groups, about $456 a year per household over the Census Bureau's 131.4 million households. Measured: Trenton, North Carolina (seed bdbb4f011961), two played years, the 18 people who gave gave a mean of $449.42 a year (scripts/core2-year/giving-proof.ts). Givers choose to give about 80 times a year, where real donors give a few times; the share is set for the yearly total.

spread.unit: share of spare cash per gift
spread.citation: Within this range a played year's mean yearly giving per giver stays within about a third to five times the Giving USA per-household figure.

volunteerHours.citation: Hours of one volunteering act for a cause group: one participant-day of volunteering. BLS American Time Use Survey 2025, Table 1, https://www.bls.gov/news.release/atus.t01.htm: volunteering (organizational and civic activities), 2.18 hours a day for those who volunteered that day (5.3% of people on an average day). Research file data/research/people/atus-2025-volunteering.json, checked by scripts/research/people-parameters-check.ts.

spread.citation: The same table: women 2.16, men 2.20.

driveConfrontHours.citation: Time spent confronting the person a grudge is held against. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No measured duration for interpersonal confrontations has been identified.

grudgeRelationshipChange.citation: Relationship level lost on each confrontation. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No measured bound in this relationship unit has been identified.

confrontImpulse.citation: Stress and mood impulse the confronted person receives. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No measured bound for this impulse on the core2 affect scale has been identified.

grudgeConfrontRecencyWeight.citation: How strongly having just confronted the person a grudge is held against weighs against confronting them again (a reason in the chooser, fading at grudgeConfrontRecencyDays). Without it a laid-off holder, whose stress and unmet safety the act answers, confronted the same person several times a day for months (179 confrontations on 179 days for one grudge in Rockport, Texas, seed cbf9ae5a6ee7, where a confrontation's other reasons summed to about 3.2). Checked so a grudge leads to an occasional confrontation, not a daily one, in a played year.

spread.reason: No study measures confrontation spacing on the chooser's utility scale.

grudgeConfrontRecencyDays.citation: Days over which the weight of a recent confrontation against another fades by a factor of e (about two-thirds gone after two months).

spread.reason: No study measures how long people wait before confronting the same person again.

causeGivenWeight.citation: How strongly what a person has lately given to their causes (volunteer sessions, donations, groups joined, causes shared, each one act, fading at causeGivenDays) weighs against a further act of the same kind (a reason in the chooser). Without it the cause acts scored the same pull each day, so in Bedford, Wyoming (seed 9a4dd331ace7) the third year's 63 volunteers gave a median of 158 sessions, about 340 hours, and 46 donors gave a median of 227 times. Set beside the Census Bureau's hours per formal volunteer (median 24 to 40 hours a year, CEV 2017 to 2023) in a played town's third year, as an exploratory proxy: the survey counts every formal volunteer through any organization, the game only cause volunteering.

spread.reason: No study measures giving on the chooser's utility scale; the volunteer-hours measure is a broader proxy for the town's totals, not a band.

causeGivenDays.citation: Days over which what a person gave to a cause fades by a factor of e in the weight against giving more (about two-thirds gone after a month).

spread.reason: No study measures how the memory of one's own giving fades; the volunteer-hours measure is a broader proxy for the town's totals, not a band.

causeJoinedDays.citation: Days over which joining a cause group fades by a factor of e in the weight against joining another (causeGivenWeight): a membership is a standing commitment, remembered for about a year, not a month. Set beside the share of people who belong to any group or organization (CEV 2017 to 2023, 23.8 to 27.1 percent) and the groups each member holds in a played town's third year, as an exploratory proxy: the survey counts any group, the game only cause groups.

spread.reason: No study measures how long one membership weighs against the next; the membership share is a broader proxy for the town's totals, not a band.

responseCarryOnFit.citation: How strongly a perceived event pushes a person toward carrying on with ordinary life and grieving privately, before their traits lean them; carrying on is the default response. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: The share of bereaved or harmed people who take up a cause is an outcome target for the whole decision, not a bound on this fit.

responseTraitLeanGain.citation: How much a person's trait lean toward a response's act kinds (the shared trait-act table) scales the event's push toward it. Starting value equals the recorded trait scale (traitScale, 3): generated people carry trait values of one on that scale, so the shared table's lean reaches a third of its range, and this gain restores the full range. P10 prototype starting value; calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No instrument-matched bound links trait-act lean to response choice after life events.

responseBereavementFitScale.citation: How much harder a death in the family pushes toward a lasting drive than the responses' own fits say: a multiple of the cause, guard and calling fits in the two bereavement rules only. Cause-sharing and speeches keep the fits as they are, because doubling them for every event would raise the causes people take up from hearing of one from 7% to 39% (replay of recorded played-year responses). Calibrated Oct 24 (traits lead) to the share of the bereaved who carry on: 65.7% resilient after a potential trauma, 95% interval 61.6 to 69.8 (Galatzer-Levy, Huang and Bonanno 2018, data/research/people/trauma-trajectories-2018.json; the spousal-loss cohort alone was 45.9%, Bonanno and others 2002, data/research/people/bonanno-bereavement-patterns-2002.json). Measured: 1,000 bereaved adults with generated temperaments (src/core2/drives.test.ts, seed p10-drives-bands) 64.1% carry on; played years at this value, 41 drawn places, 636 of 950 bereaved adults (family and household of the person who died, 16 and older) carried on, 66.9% (95% interval 63.9 to 69.9). At 2.0 the played share read 69.9% and at 2.05 71.3% in earlier pooled batches, hence 2.1.

spread.citation: In the fixture a scale of 1.9 gives 70.9% and 2.2 gives 60.1% of the bereaved carrying on against the 61.6 to 69.8% band; replaying 341 recorded bereaved responses from played years, the share stays inside the band from about 2.0 to 2.25.

responseAgencyTurnAge.citation: Age at which a person's capacity to form a lasting drive of their own from an event is half of an adult's, rising smoothly (logistic) around it; starting value near the ages when adolescents form durable civic identities and two years below the age of majority. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: Developmental studies describe identity formation across adolescence, not a measured midpoint for event-born drives.

responseAgencyWidthYears.citation: Width in years of the smooth rise in drive-forming capacity around the turn age. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No measured width for this rise has been identified.

responseRetrainAgeCenter.citation: Age at which the logistic fall in a displaced worker's capacity to retrain or start over has reached one half. Jacobson, LaLonde and Sullivan 2005 (Journal of Econometrics; Chicago Fed WP 2003-25): of displaced workers, 16.8% of men under 35 against 10.9% at 35 and over, and 23.5% of women under 35 against 17.2%, completed community-college credit, so the older group retrains at about 0.65 to 0.73 of the younger group's rate. See data/research/drives/economic-losses.json. Set to 40 on Oct 25 (M0-M2 lead) with a width of 18 years: a 45-year-old keeps 0.65 of a 28-year-old's capacity, the low end of the paper's ratio, a 35-year-old 0.86 and a 58-year-old 0.41.
responseRetrainAgeCenter.estimatedFrom: The under-35 and 35-and-over completion rates in Jacobson, LaLonde and Sullivan 2005, read at the groups' typical ages (28 and 45); the paper gives two age groups, not a curve. Center and width were then set together with responseAmbitionFit so that the unchanged M1-11 check and drives-economy.test.ts read inside 6-25% in the generated towns listed under responseAmbitionFit.

spread.citation: At a width of 18, a center of 35 gives a 0.61 ratio between 28 and 45 and 60 gives 0.81, which brackets the paper's 0.65 to 0.73.

responseRetrainAgeWidthYears.citation: Width in years of the smooth fall in capacity to retrain or start over around responseRetrainAgeCenter. Jacobson, LaLonde and Sullivan 2005 report two age groups: of displaced workers, 16.8% of men under 35 against 10.9% at 35 and over, and 23.5% of women under 35 against 17.2%, completed community-college credit, so the older group retrains at about 0.65 to 0.73 of the younger group's rate. That ratio is of outcomes, not of capacity: the response competes with carrying on in a near tie, so a fall in capacity becomes a much steeper fall in who chooses it. Set to 60 on Oct 28 (red-main owner) from played years: at 18, with layoffs read by tenure since Oct 27 (recent hires go first, so most displaced workers are young), under-35s chose it 47%, 45% and 57% and those 35 and over 9%, 4% and 2% in Austin, Minnesota (2702908), Washington, District of Columbia (1150000) and Murdo, South Dakota (4644260), and M1-11 read over its ceiling; at 60, with the fit unchanged, under-35s read 23.7% pooled (75 of 316) and those 35 and over 7.3% (14 of 191), the towns 19.4%, 15.1% and 14.7%. The older group still reads under the paper's 11-17%: the rest of the gap is in what else the choice reads (the money need presses younger workers harder), not this curve.
responseRetrainAgeWidthYears.estimatedFrom: The paper's two age groups as outcome shares, read in played years of buildBenchWorld with every module (the M1-11 check), since the curve's effect on the outcome runs through the choice between responses.

spread.citation: Measured outcome ratios, 35 and over to under 35, in the three towns above: 0.11 at a width of 18 and 0.31 at 60. A width under 40 steepens the cliff the ratio fell from; past 80 the curve is nearly flat and the fit alone sets the share.

responseCarryOnBaseline.citation: Ordinary life's own pull toward carrying on, independent of the event; a weak event or a person with little agency leaves life as it was. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: The share of bereaved or harmed people who take up a cause is an outcome target for the whole decision, not a bound on this baseline.

driveStrengthScale.citation: How quickly a response's urgency fills a drive toward its ceiling of one: strength rises as one minus the unfilled share times e to the minus urgency times this scale, so drives stay on the same unit as needs. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: No measured bound links event urgency to the strength of a resulting drive.

driveRetireStrength.citation: Strength below which a faded drive stops being rewritten each day; its effect on choices is already negligible and it rejoins if a new event renews the topic. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: A storage floor for speed, not a behavioral quantity; no empirical bound applies.

driveTraceRetention.citation: Most recent decision and act traces the drives module keeps in memory for observers; counts are always exact. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: A memory budget for developer traces, not a behavioral quantity; no empirical bound applies.

responseCauseFit.citation: How strongly a perceived event pushes toward taking up a cause about its topic, before traits lean the person; below the carry-on fit so that only leaning traits form a drive. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: The share of bereaved or harmed people who take up a cause is an outcome target for the whole decision, not a bound on this fit.

responseGrudgeFit.citation: How strongly a perceived wrong pushes toward holding a grudge against the person responsible, before traits lean the person. Calibrated Oct 24 (traits lead) so the share of laid-off workers who hold a grudge sits inside the share of fired workers who act on one: 1.7 to 14.9% filed a claim, between those given a complete explanation or treated with dignity and those given none or treated without (Greenberg, Lind, Scott and Welchans 1998, data/research/people/termination-claims-1998.json; the share who hold a grudge is not published and a claim is the costly end of one), and under the 69% of the fired who call their firing unfair (NELP and YouGov 2022, data/research/people/nelp-yougov-firings-2022.json). The prototype value 0.8 gave 0.2% of laid-off adults a grudge, so none was ever held and relationships.fall-out never ran. Measured: 1,000 laid-off adults with generated temperaments (src/core2/drives.test.ts, seed p10-drives-bands) 12.0%; played years at this value, 14 drawn places, 38 of 403 layoff and closure responses held a grudge, 9.4% (95% interval 6.9 to 12.7).

spread.citation: In the same fixture a fit of 1.3 gives 4.4% and 1.8 gives 14.6% of laid-off adults a grudge; replaying 377 recorded layoff responses from played years, 1.3 gives 2.7% and 1.9 gives 14.9%: inside 1.7 to 14.9% from about 1.3 to 1.8.

responseGuardFit.citation: How strongly a perceived event pushes toward a resolve to protect one's family, before traits lean the person; below the carry-on fit so that only leaning traits form a drive. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: The share of bereaved or harmed people who take up a cause is an outcome target for the whole decision, not a bound on this fit.

responseSecureHomeFit.citation: How strongly losing a home, or facing an eviction, pushes toward a resolve to secure a home again. Carrying on keeps its baseline (responseCarryOnBaseline), so a fit near 3 lets most people form the resolve while those whose traits lean toward keeping things the same carry on (owner, Oct 14: 'not being homeless is some people's motivation'). Measured: Washington, D.C. (seed 646c5d940e1a), a home loss given to 7 jobless adults on February 19, 2025 (dev mode): 5 formed it and 2 carried on; at 1.5, 1 of 7; at 4.0, 7 of 7.

spread.citation: From one in three forming it to all of them, in the same check.

responseAmbitionFit.citation: How strongly a perceived loss pushes toward an ambition to prove oneself (retraining, a new business), before traits lean the person. Calibrated Oct 12 (OPUS-PEOPLE) so that, when every employer in a generated town closes, the share of workers who form this drive matches displaced-worker research: about 10-16% complete retraining (Jacobson, LaLonde and Sullivan 2005) and entrepreneurship rises 2-4 points (Roed and Skogstrom 2014); see data/research/drives/economic-losses.json. Tuned on seeds c1 and c2 (fit 2.0: 17%); checked on fresh seeds c3 and c4: 42 of 329 workers (12.8%). Recalibrated Oct 24 (M0-M2 lead): after the Oct 13 traits change that gave every trait a low side (#4060) the same fit of 1.9 gave 26 to 32% in drawn towns; 1.5 gives 12 to 17% in Riverdale, Georgia, Warren, Illinois, Excelsior, Minnesota and Flora, Illinois. Recalibrated Oct 25 (M0-M2 lead) with the retraining age fade (responseRetrainAgeCenter): North Canton, Ohio read 35.1% at 1.5 because 77 of its 103 job losses came from one wholesale employer and its full workers leaned toward ambition; with the age fade, 1.75 read 19.1% there and 7.8% in Steamboat Springs, Colorado. Recalibrated again Oct 25 (M0-M2 lead) after Manson, Iowa (1948990, seed b63a9c1eccbba0f45589110cb2c6924003d0e8b668b9298a1bde2302f0d6df98) read 1 of 25 at 1.85: the retraining age fade was changed to a center of 40 and a width of 18 (a gentler fall, the 28-to-45 ratio at the paper's low end) and the fit raised to 3.4, because the fit now multiplies a capacity of 0.66 at age 28 (an effective 2.2 for a young adult). Read by the unchanged M1-11 check at 3.4: Manson, Iowa 2 of 25 (8.0%), North Canton, Ohio 28 of 118 (23.7%), Steamboat Springs, Colorado 75 of 555 (13.5%; 9.9% on main at 1.5 with no fade), and three towns drawn from a root written down first (wt72-accept-2026-10-25-a): Washington, District of Columbia 10 of 68 (14.7%), Franklin, North Carolina 17 of 72 (23.6%) and Magnolia, New Jersey 5 of 40 (12.5%). drives-economy.test.ts (Christmas, Florida, where every employer closes and the workers average 51) reads 15 of 215 (7.0%). The response competes with carry-on, whose baseline does not scale with the loss, and most workers' losses press about equally hard, so a town's share moves quickly with this value; it was set from the pooled share over six towns (13.5%) and every town was then checked. Full people who answer a layoff choose it two to four times as often as counted people in the same town (North Canton at fit 2.45: 8 of 15 against 16 of 103; Steamboat Springs 18 of 66 against 48 of 489), which is why a town's share also follows its mix of the two. Kept at 3.4 on Oct 28 (red-main owner) when the retraining fade's width went from 18 to 60 years: with layoffs read by tenure the displaced skew young, and at 18 the young read about half and the town shares 30-41% (M1-11 red in seven drawn towns); at 60 Austin, Minnesota read 19.4%, Washington, District of Columbia 15.1% and Murdo, South Dakota 14.7% (see responseRetrainAgeWidthYears).

spread.reason: With the retraining age fade, 3.4 gives 7% to 24% of displaced workers in seven generated towns (Manson, Iowa; North Canton, Ohio; Steamboat Springs, Colorado; Washington, District of Columbia; Franklin, North Carolina; Magnolia, New Jersey; Christmas, Florida); the research band is 10-16% retraining plus a few points of new businesses.

responseCallingFit.citation: How strongly a perceived event pushes toward a calling to serve others; lower than a cause because a calling commits a person to lasting service rather than to one condition, before traits lean the person; below the carry-on fit so that only leaning traits form a drive. P10 prototype starting value; no direct source for this coefficient. Calibration against P9 life replays and bereaved/activist cohort spreads is pending and blocks release.

spread.reason: The share of bereaved or harmed people who take up a cause is an outcome target for the whole decision, not a bound on this fit.

resilienceBaseRateScale.citation: Scale (0.097 since Oct 27, 2026; 0.087 from Oct 21; 0.106 before) at which the SSA 2023 period life table hazard counts against each person's resilience line, with the recorded chronic-condition weights (data/research/health/chronic-condition-pack-2026.json) multiplying it, chosen so expected yearly deaths match the life table applied to the same residents.
resilienceBaseRateScale.estimatedFrom: Refit Oct 27, 2026 on the head of claude/health-resilience over twenty-four generated towns (scripts/health/mortality-band.ts, seeds sr1 to sr16 and m01 to m08, one played year each, default size, no place chosen): at 0.087 they recorded 400 deaths against 446.0 expected (ratio 0.897; sr1 to sr16 286 against 297.9, 0.96; m01 to m08 114 against 148.1, 0.77); at 0.097 they record 450 deaths against 446.0 expected (ratio 1.009, band 0.8 to 1.2; sr1 to sr16 325 against 297.9, 1.091; m01 to m08 125 against 148.1, 0.844). The Oct 21 refit (0.087, sixteen towns, 319 against 297.9) was taken before the chronic-condition weights were restored to 0.065. Totals only; no person's outcome is set by it. Single towns range from 0.3 to 1.9 of the table's count at a year (about 19 expected deaths each), so one town says little; the places differ by more than chance, which the single scale and the unrefit condition weights do not model.

resilienceHashDigits.citation: Half of the existing stable hash's sixteen hexadecimal digits (64-bit FNV-1a, src/core2/kernel/ids.ts); two 32-bit halves feed the existing fixed-point survival-line helper (src/core2/kernel/fixed-point.ts). A generation key, not a behavioral draw.

driveClosureImpulse.citation: Losing one's job, to a closure or a layoff: the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's 'Fired at work', 47 life-change units divided by 100 (Holmes and Rahe 1967, Journal of Psychosomatic Research 11(2):213-218), the same anchor the story director uses for a lost job.
driveClosureImpulse.estimatedFrom: Holmes and Rahe (1967) Social Readjustment Rating Scale; spread 0.39 to 0.47 (the scale's 'business readjustment' to 'fired at work')

driveEvictionImpulse.citation: Losing one's home to eviction, sized like losing one's job: the Social Readjustment Rating Scale has no eviction item (its nearest, 'Foreclosure of mortgage or loan', is 30 life-change units; 'Fired at work' is 47; Holmes and Rahe 1967), and Desmond and Kimbro (2015, Social Forces 94(1):295-324) find evicted mothers' depression twice that of matched mothers, so the foreclosure item understates it. At 0.30 no one of 101 evicted residents in a drawn town formed a drive; at 0.47, 6 to 8% hold a grudge against the landlord.
driveEvictionImpulse.estimatedFrom: Holmes and Rahe (1967) and Desmond and Kimbro (2015); spread 0.3 to 0.47

driveHomeLostImpulse.citation: Losing one's home (doubled up with kin, in a shelter or on the street), sized like an eviction (driveEvictionImpulse): the Social Readjustment Rating Scale's nearest items are 'Foreclosure of mortgage or loan' at 30 and 'Fired at work' at 47 life-change units (Holmes and Rahe 1967), and homelessness follows the eviction that caused it.
driveHomeLostImpulse.estimatedFrom: Holmes and Rahe (1967), as for driveEvictionImpulse; spread 0.3 to 0.6

healthShelteredHazardFactor.citation: How much faster strain toward serious illness and death builds for a person in a homeless shelter. Homeless people in high-income countries die at two to five times the rate of the general population (Fazel, Geddes and Kushel 2014, 'The health of homeless people in high-income countries', The Lancet 384(9953):1529-1540); sheltered people sit at the low end.
healthShelteredHazardFactor.estimatedFrom: Fazel, Geddes and Kushel (2014); the low end of their range for sheltered adults

spread.citation: Within Fazel et al.'s range for sheltered adults.

healthUnshelteredHazardFactor.citation: How much faster strain builds for a person sleeping outside: the upper part of Fazel et al.'s two-to-five-times range, because unsheltered adults die at higher rates than sheltered ones (Roncarati et al. 2018, 'Mortality Among Unsheltered Homeless Adults in Boston, Massachusetts, 2000-2009', JAMA Internal Medicine 178(9):1242-1248).
healthUnshelteredHazardFactor.estimatedFrom: Fazel, Geddes and Kushel (2014) and Roncarati et al. (2018)

spread.citation: The upper half of Fazel et al.'s range.

healthDoubledUpHazardFactor.citation: How much faster strain builds for a person doubled up with relatives after losing their home: crowded and unstable housing raises the risk of illness, well short of a shelter's (the sheltered factor's lower bound is 1.5).

spread.citation: From no change to the sheltered factor's low end.

healthEvictionHazardFactor.citation: How much faster strain builds in the years after an eviction: eviction raises hospital and emergency department use and lowers earnings for about two years (Collinson, Humphries, Mader, Reed, Tannenbaum and van Dijk 2024, 'Eviction and Poverty in American Cities', The Quarterly Journal of Economics 139(1):57-120).
healthEvictionHazardFactor.estimatedFrom: Collinson et al. (2024); a modest rise, as their effects on health care use are modest

spread.citation: From no change to a third higher.

healthEvictionEffectDays.citation: How long an eviction's effect on health lasts: about two years after the filing (Collinson et al. 2024).

spread.citation: One to three years.

livingCostWriteOffBills.citation: FFIEC, Uniform Retail Credit Classification and Account Management Policy (2000): closed-end retail credit is charged off at 120 days past due and open-end credit at 180 days; a month's bill is the unit here.
livingCostWriteOffBills.estimatedFrom: 120 days past due is four monthly bills; open-end accounts at 180 days would be six. A household's outside living costs (utilities, phone, insurance and the like) are written off after about four unpaid bills.

spread.unit: monthly bills unpaid before the debt is written off
spread.citation: Utility disconnection and collection practice (about 60 to 90 days) to the FFIEC open-end charge-off age (180 days).

supplierTradeTermsDays.citation: Net 30 is the most common U.S. business-to-business invoice term; Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta / Small Business Credit Survey and trade-credit literature (e.g., Petersen and Rajan 1997, Review of Financial Studies 10(3)) describe 30-day terms as the norm.
supplierTradeTermsDays.estimatedFrom: Outside supplier bills for a firm's costs are paid one month after the sales that incur them; spread 10 to 60 days across industries.

fullTimeWeeklyHours.citation: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey concepts and definitions: full-time workers usually work 35 hours or more a week at all jobs; https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm#fullparttime

openingPartTimeOlderWorkerAge.citation: BLS CPS 2021 annual averages, Table 8 'Employed and unemployed full- and part-time workers by age, sex, race, and Hispanic or Latino ethnicity': part-time work is far more common among employed people 65 and over than among those 25 to 54; https://www.bls.gov/cps/aa2021/cpsaat08.htm
openingPartTimeOlderWorkerAge.estimatedFrom: The town generator's existing rule: an employed resident 65 or over works part-time. A single age cut, not the CPS age gradient.

spread.citation: Social Security early and latest-credit claiming ages bracketing the shift toward part-time work.

openingFullTimeWeeklyHours.citation: BLS Current Population Survey 2021 annual averages, Table 19 'Persons at work in agriculture and related and in nonagricultural industries by hours of work': people usually working full time averaged about 42 to 43 hours a week at work; https://www.bls.gov/cps/aa2021/cpsaat19.htm
openingFullTimeWeeklyHours.estimatedFrom: A full-time job copied from a part-time recorded role gets the midpoint of the town generator's full-time range (35–45 hours), slightly under the CPS average hours at work.

spread.citation: The town generator's full-time range; 35 is the BLS full-time threshold.

openingPartTimeWeeklyHours.citation: BLS Current Population Survey 2021 annual averages, Table 19 'Persons at work in agriculture and related and in nonagricultural industries by hours of work': people usually working part time averaged about 22 to 23 hours a week at work; https://www.bls.gov/cps/aa2021/cpsaat19.htm
openingPartTimeWeeklyHours.estimatedFrom: A part-time job copied from a full-time recorded role gets the midpoint of the town generator's part-time range (16–29 hours).

spread.citation: The town generator's part-time range.

openingPartTimeShiftMinutes.citation: The town schedule generator's part-time shift (the old engine's work-schedules.ts), consistent with CPS part-time averages of about 22–23 hours over four days.
openingPartTimeShiftMinutes.estimatedFrom: Shifts longer than six hours are cut to five and a half hours for part-time staff, as the generator does.

spread.citation: Four- to six-hour shifts.

residentsOutlayShareOfIncome.citation: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, NIPA Table 2.1 'Personal Income and Its Disposition', 2019 annual: personal outlays about $15.6 trillion of personal income about $18.6 trillion (taxes about $2.2 trillion, saving 7.3% of disposable income); https://apps.bea.gov/iTable/?reqid=19&step=2&isuri=1&categories=survey#eyJhcHBpZCI6MTksInN0ZXBzIjpbMSwyLDNdLCJkYXRhIjpbWyJjYXRlZ29yaWVzIiwiU3VydmV5Il0sWyJOSVBBX1RhYmxlX0xpc3QiLCI1OCJdXX0=
residentsOutlayShareOfIncome.estimatedFrom: Counted households spend this share of last month's income; the rest stands for taxes and saving until income taxes are collected from the counts. 2019 is used rather than 2020–2021, when stimulus and closures pushed saving far above normal.

spread.citation: BEA NIPA Table 2.1, 2020 (pandemic low) to 2022 (low saving).

residentsIncomeWindowMonths.citation: Households smooth spending over income swings (permanent-income behavior); a quarter evens out four- and five-payday months and monthly owner payouts.

spread.citation: From reacting to each month's income to spending from a year's average.

sellerCapacityUtilization.citation: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, G.17 Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization: total industry capacity utilization averaged 79.6% over 1972–2023; https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g17/current/
sellerCapacityUtilization.estimatedFrom: A seller's monthly capacity is its projected sales divided by this rate; spending beyond it buys the same thing outside the town (residents travel to the next town). Industrial utilization stands in for retail and service capacity.

spread.citation: G.17 range over business cycles, 1972–2023.

openingRetirementClaimAnchorYearsBeforeF.citation: Calibrated so the opening's retirees claimed at SSA's average age at entitlement, 63.4–65.0 for claims made 2000–2020 (SSA Annual Statistical Supplement 2021, Table 6.B5.1).

spread.citation: From claiming at full retirement age to the earliest claim.

openingRetirementClaimAnchorYearsBeforeF.checkedAgainst: Measured once over three generated openings (seeds claim-a/b/c, 3,694 retirees): mean claim age 64.08 (SSA 63.4–65.0), 20% at 62 (SSA 2021 about 25%); claiming at 70 (SSA about 8%) is not reached yet.

openingRetirementClaimNeedPullYears.citation: People with little saved claim early: in 2021 about a quarter of new retired workers claimed at 62 (SSA Annual Statistical Supplement 2022, Table 6.B5).

spread.citation: From no effect to claiming at 62 from any full retirement age.

openingRetirementClaimNeedPullYears.checkedAgainst: Measured once over three generated openings (seeds claim-a/b/c, 3,694 retirees): mean claim age 64.08 (SSA 63.4–65.0), 20% at 62 (SSA 2021 about 25%); claiming at 70 (SSA about 8%) is not reached yet.

openingRetirementClaimFullBufferMonths.citation: Months of living costs in cash at which savings no longer push an early claim; Federal Reserve SHED 2020: 64% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash.

spread.citation: From an emergency fund to several years of costs.

gameStartDate.citation: Inauguration Day, 20th Amendment §1; owner ruling Oct 14, 2026: every game starts on January 20, 2025, in every place. Written as year, month and day (YYYYMMDD); read it with gameStartDate() in src/core2/game-start.ts.

preStartStepMonths.citation: Owner ruling (relayed by the CTO on PR #3999, October 12, 2026): history before the start runs at coarse steps, monthly or quarterly (M1-14).

spread.citation: The two step sizes the pre-start contract offers (src/core2/pre-start.ts).

openingPupilTeacherRatio.citation: NCES, Digest of Education Statistics 2022, Table 208.20: public elementary and secondary pupil/teacher ratio, fall 2021, 15.4. https://nces.ed.gov/programs/digest/d22/tables/dt22_208.20.asp

openingPublicSchoolShare.citation: NCES Fast Facts, Back-to-school statistics: fall 2021 public school enrollment 49.4 million and private 4.7 million; NCES NHES 2019: about 2.8% of school-age children homeschooled.
openingPublicSchoolShare.estimatedFrom: 49.4 / (49.4 + 4.7 + about 1.6 homeschooled) ≈ 0.87 of school-age children enrolled in public schools; pre-K in the public count is not separated.

spread.citation: State public shares range roughly from 0.80 to 0.92 (NCES Digest Table 205.80, private enrollment by state).

openingSchoolAgeFirst.citation: NCES Digest Table 203.10 and Census school-age population: kindergarten through grade 12 serves ages 5–17.

openingSchoolAgeLast.citation: NCES Digest Table 203.10 and Census school-age population: kindergarten through grade 12 serves ages 5–17.

openingTeacherMinimumAge.citation: A bachelor's degree is required for a public school teaching license in every state (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, Kindergarten and Elementary School Teachers, How to Become One).
openingTeacherMinimumAge.estimatedFrom: Typical age at a bachelor's degree; the town generator's teacher role uses the same minimum age.

spread.citation: NCES Digest Table 104.10 age at bachelor's completion.

openingWorkingAgeLast.citation: BLS Current Population Survey, labor force participation by age (annual averages): participation falls from about 65% at ages 55–64 to about 19% at 65 and over.
openingWorkingAgeLast.estimatedFrom: New opening jobs go to adults under 65, where most of the labor force is; the opening's part-time rule already starts at 65 (openingPartTimeOlderWorkerAge).

spread.citation: Social Security earliest claim (62) to the delayed-credit end (70).

openingPrivateTuitionAnnualUsd.citation: NCES, Digest of Education Statistics 2021, Table 205.50: average tuition at all private elementary and secondary schools, 2011–12, $12,420 in constant 2020–21 dollars. https://nces.ed.gov/programs/digest/d21/tables/dt21_205.50.asp

openingCustomerClubMembershipsAnnualNati.citation: BLS, The Economics Daily, 'The new year and household spending' (2026), https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2026/the-new-year-and-household-spending.htm: Consumer Expenditure Survey, social, recreation and health club memberships, $272 per consumer unit in 2024 (2021: $212).

traitLeanScale.citation: The trait lean difference between two options that counts as a full-strength pull (1) in a formula decision. Starting value: the largest lean difference across generated adults in a 1,200-person drawn town is about 0.6 to 0.7 (OPUS-TRAITS probe, Oct 12, 2026), so the strongest personalities reach about 1, the range of the hand-picked trait sums it replaces.

spread.citation: Generated-town lean differences between options (OPUS-TRAITS probe, Oct 12, 2026): 99th percentile about 0.5, maximum about 0.7.

truthDefaultPull.citation: How strongly a hearer leans toward believing a claim they cannot check, before traits: truth-default theory (Levine 2014, Journal of Language and Social Psychology 33(4)) finds people judge most statements honest. With traitLeanScale, only hearers whose traits lean hard toward doubt (about the most suspicious tenth) doubt a lie.

spread.citation: Levine 2014: truth judgments run well above half in deception experiments; the spread keeps believers a clear majority.

believeStrangerPull.citation: How strongly a hearer leans toward believing a story or speech from a stranger with nothing to go on, before traits: truth-default theory (Levine 2014, Journal of Language and Social Psychology 33(4)) finds people judge most statements honest, so a stranger's bare word sits a little above even. With the decision's weight (traitWeightConversationBelieveClaim), only hearers whose traits lean hard toward doubt (about the most suspicious tenth) doubt a stranger's claim; a teller the hearer is close to (believeClosenessWeight) and a claim that fits where the hearer already leans (believeFitWeight) add to it, so about 95% of the stories and speeches heard in a played election-window year (Halfway, Missouri, seed 3e9ed70a5fb7) are taken in. The player's own claims in a conversation are still read by the director's doubtsClaim at truthDefaultPull (SG-TRAITS-director-claims-reader).

spread.citation: Levine 2014: truth judgments run well above half in deception experiments; the spread keeps a stranger's word believed by a clear majority.

believeClosenessWeight.citation: How much the closeness of a teller to the hearer (0 to 1, the one closeness read, closenessBetween) adds to taking a claim in: people take the word of those close to them (Levine 2014 truth-default theory names a prior relationship as a main reason the default is not overturned). No study gives the size against the hearer's temperament; it is set so a hearer who leans hard toward doubt still believes a tie as faint as a first conversation (closeness about 0.1 adds 0.3, twice the largest trait term) and the typical contact (closeness about 0.25) carries the claim.

spread.unit: scaled trait lean per unit of closeness
spread.citation: Checked so a close friend or relative is believed by every hearer and a stranger's word is left to the hearer's temperament and what the claim argues.

believeFitWeight.citation: How much a claim that argues the way the hearer already leans (their current view on its question times the side it argues, -1 to 1) adds to taking it in, and one that argues against subtracts: people accept claims that fit their prior views more readily (motivated reasoning; Kunda 1990, Psychological Bulletin 108(3)). No study gives the size; it is set so a claim that argues hard against a hearer's view (fit -0.5) is doubted even from a fairly close tie, as the closeness weight alone would carry it.

spread.unit: scaled trait lean per unit of fit
spread.citation: Checked so fit moves a hearing by about as much as a middling tie does (believeClosenessWeight times a closeness of about 0.5).

siblingBirthGapDays.citation: The fewest days between two siblings' births in a household the opening draws: nine months, the owner's floor for siblings who are not twins (playtest, Oct 24, 2026, play-stop-20: siblings born at least nine months apart). A pregnancy begun right after a birth and carried to term, 39 to 40 weeks (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, Committee Opinion 579, Definition of Term Pregnancy, 2013), ends 273 to 280 days later.

spread.citation: From a late-preterm birth at 35 weeks to a full-term birth a few weeks after a pregnancy begun at once.

minimumParentAgeAtBirth.citation: The youngest age at which a household's adult is recorded as a child's parent: the Census Bureau's fertility tables count children ever born from age 15 (U.S. Census Bureau, Table 1. Women's Number of Children Ever Born by Age and Marital Status: June 2018, the source of src/core2/data/opening-kin.json fertilityByAge). A younger adult in the home is a sibling or other relative.

traitDecisionWeight.citation: How much a person's scaled trait lean between two options (about -1 to 1, traitLeanScale) adds to a government or civic decision's score when the site has no trait weight of its own (OPUS-TRAITS, Oct 12, 2026). Half a full-strength pull: traits tilt the choice without overriding the record, party and money reasons the site already weighs.

spread.unit: score per unit of scaled trait lean
spread.citation: Starting range; the site reasons it joins run about -1 to 1 (views, warmth, grievance), so the trait term stays a minority share of the total.

circleDecisionDetailDays.citation: How long a circle member's act keeps every option's score before only its chosen reasons remain. Set to the spread's low end: at 30 days a played year in a large town (South Burlington, Vermont) held 2,904 MB against the 2,000 MB memory bound, most of it these kept scores.

spread.citation: A week (the routine retention window, routineRetentionDays) to a season; checked against the memory guard and the 'why' view.

playerDecisionDetailDays.citation: How long the player's own routine act keeps every option's score before only its chosen reasons remain; after a year the summary and reasons are kept, not every detail.

spread.citation: Half a year to two years; checked against the memory guard (scripts/core2-guard/memory.mjs) and the 'why' view.

circleActRetentionMonths.citation: Owner ruling, Oct 12 (running memory stays small: keep current state, each person's key facts and recent detail; summarize or drop old detail): how long a circle member's routine act stays in the log after its reasons are condensed.

spread.citation: A season to a three-year term; checked against the memory check (scripts/core2-guard/memory.mjs) and the journal.

experiencedKeyRetentionDays.citation: Owner ruling, Oct 12 (running memory stays small): how long a person keeps the bare 'I lived through this event' key after the day, once it is no longer the source of a drive they hold. Its only readers are the same-day appraisal and a drive's update; the event's own facts stay.

spread.citation: A month to a year; checked against the 450-day play digest (unchanged) and the yearly heap in scripts/core2-year/years-profile.ts.

openingTeacherAnnualWageUsd.citation: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2025, national median annual wage for the game's teacher occupation (profession:teacher), as the town pay table records it (the old engine's town-pay.ts, nationalMedianAnnualWage). Used only where a town has no recorded teacher job to copy.

openingTeacherHoursDaily.citation: A full-time teacher's school day where the town has no recorded teacher to copy; the town generator's recorded teacher roles are the reference.

spread.citation: From a 7-hour to an 8.5-hour school day; checked against the town generator's recorded teacher roles.

unauthorizedShareOfNoncitizens.citation: Pew Research Center, 'What we know about unauthorized immigrants living in the U.S.' (July 22, 2024; https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/07/22/what-we-know-about-unauthorized-immigrants-living-in-the-us/), from the 2022 American Community Survey: 'The unauthorized immigrant population in the United States grew to 11.0 million in 2022', which is '23% of the foreign-born population', and 'in 2022, 49% of all immigrants in the country were naturalized U.S. citizens'. Noncitizens are then 51% of about 47.8 million immigrants, about 24.4 million, of whom 11.0 million are unauthorized: 0.45. Read by the jobs engine (src/core2/jobs-web.ts) through isUnauthorized in src/core2/citizenship.ts.
unauthorizedShareOfNoncitizens.estimatedFrom: 11.0 million unauthorized over (11.0 / 0.23) x 0.51 noncitizen immigrants, national, 2022.

spread.unit: share of noncitizens without work authorization
spread.citation: States differ: Pew's same report puts 42% of unauthorized immigrants in California and Texas, where the share of noncitizens is higher than in states whose noncitizens are mostly lawful permanent residents; Pew's August 2025 revision of the 2022 total moves the national share by a few points.

citizenShareStatePriorAdults.citation: How many adults' worth of the state's CPS citizen share a place's ACS share is blended with, so a small place's noisy sample (ACS 5-year margins) leans on its state.

spread.citation: From trusting a place of a few hundred adults nearly fully to leaning on the state until a place has thousands of adults.

budgetNewGameLoadSeconds.citation: Owner, M7 work order (docs/packages/M7-early-access.md): a new game loads within two minutes while the loading story plays.

spread.citation: The owner's two-minute ceiling; lower is better.

budgetYearSeconds.citation: Owner rule (AGENTS.md, Speed): a town's game year must run in under two minutes.

spread.citation: The owner's two-minute ceiling; lower is better.

budgetSlowestDaySeconds.citation: M7-01: a day advances without visible waiting; the slowest day of a played year must stay under this.

spread.citation: From an instant-feeling day to the longest a player waits without a progress indicator.

budgetSaveCompressedMegabytes.citation: M7-01 save-size budget: The Political Process's saves are 23 to 28 MB at any game length (owner's saves, BOARD Oct 12); ours must stay nowhere near 1.6 GB.

spread.citation: From The Political Process's size to four times it.

schoolDayHours.citation: NCES Schools and Staffing Survey 2011–12: public schools' average school day was about 6.7 hours.
schoolDayHours.estimatedFrom: The national average length of a public school day, used for every school.

spread.citation: Typical public school days across states and districts.

willAgeWeight.citation: How much each year past willAgeMidpointYears adds to a person's lean toward having made a will, in midpoint-lengths: older people far more often have one. Checked against Gallup (May 2016, 'Majority in U.S. Do Not Have a Will'): 44% of U.S. adults have a will, rising with age to about two in three past 65.

spread.citation: From a gentle rise with age to most older adults having one.

willAgeMidpointYears.citation: The age at which a person with no lean either way is as likely to have made a will as not; with the trait lean averaging zero, about half of 50-year-olds have one, between Gallup's 44% of all adults and its two in three past 65 (Gallup, May 2016).

spread.citation: Ages where Gallup's share of will-holders crosses one half.

probateDays.citation: How long an estate waits in probate before the heirs take: most estates take six months to a year, longer when contested (American Bar Association, 'Guide to Wills and Estates', probate chapter).
probateDays.estimatedFrom: ABA guidance: six months to a year; nine months used

spread.citation: Six months to eighteen months.

trustWealthMidpointMinor.citation: The estate, in cents, at which a person with no lean either way is as likely to have set up a living trust as not, and at which half of it sits in the trust. Few families hold trusts and holding rises steeply with wealth (Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2022, trust and managed-assets questions); the midpoint is placed near the wealth of the top few percent, an estimate and not a reading of any table.
trustWealthMidpointMinor.estimatedFrom: The Survey of Consumer Finances' pattern of trust holding by wealth, placed at about five million dollars

spread.citation: From one million to ten million dollars.

trustWealthWeight.citation: How much each e-fold of an estate past trustWealthMidpointMinor adds to a person's lean toward having set up a living trust. Trust holding climbs from rare among ordinary families to common among the very wealthy (Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2022).

spread.citation: From a gentle rise with wealth to most of the very wealthy holding a trust.

playerEntryAge.citation: The turn-18 golden path's player entry age (AGENTS.md). The opening keeps at least one full resident of this age when one occurs in the place's generated households, selecting a household to keep full rather than creating an age cohort the place lacks. Matches the bench player's default entry age (src/bench/world.ts).

spread.citation: Design sensitivity bounds around the turn-18 start, from 17 through 21 years.

cohortSearchMinimumHouseholds.citation: How many households the opening draws, at least, to find one holding a child of the player's cohort age in a town whose own sample shows none. Measured Oct 15, 2026: in Freedom Acres, Arizona, Princeton, Arkansas (Census population 3) and Danvers, Montana (population 6), a family with a child of age 17 turned up within 8 to 23 further draws; the old cap, the town's own household count, was 3 to 36.

spread.citation: From about four times the longest search measured to the point a draw costs a visible fraction of the opening's build time.

careNeedHalfExcessHazard.citation: The combined chronic-condition hazard weight above ordinary health (the weight that sets a person's illness onset) that asks for half of full care from a relative at home. A grown relative's care need is excess / (excess + this). Checked on three generated towns over 90 days (seeds care-a, care-b, care-c; Filley, Nebraska; Slaughter Beach and Ardencroft, Delaware): values of 3 and 6 gave the same share of person-days caring for household members (21.5%, 3.4% and 48.8%, against 18.8%, 0.2% and 43.6% with children alone; ATUS 2025 Table 1 household care 22.0% of person-days), because a relative who asks for any care draws the act; the value sets how strongly. No direct source for the value itself. Outcome bands it is checked against: ATUS Table A-1, caring for and helping household adults, 4.6 to 6.2 percent of people a day (2018 to 2025), and caring for and helping household members, 21.6 to 24.1 percent (data/research/core/bls-atus-table-a1-2025.json, reported by scripts/research/content-year.ts).

spread.reason: Calibrated to one ATUS share; no empirical range for how much condition hazard asks for care in these score units.

healthWorkerContributionSingleAnnualUsd.citation: KFF, 2024 Employer Health Benefits Survey: covered workers with single coverage contributed an average of $1,368 a year (https://www.kff.org/health-costs/2024-employer-health-benefits-survey/), read through search results on 2026-10-20; not the survey's own page.

healthWorkerContributionFamilyAnnualUsd.citation: KFF, 2024 Employer Health Benefits Survey: covered workers with family coverage contributed an average of $6,296 a year, out of an average family premium of $25,572 (https://www.kff.org/health-costs/2024-employer-health-benefits-survey/), read through search results on 2026-10-20; not the survey's own page.

healthEmployerPolicyholderShare.citation: The share of employed working-age adults who hold an employer plan in their own name. Not read directly from any table.
healthEmployerPolicyholderShare.estimatedFrom: The Census Bureau's Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2023 (P60-284) puts employment-based coverage at 53.7 percent of the whole population, dependents included, and the KFF 2024 survey shows most covered workers also cover family members; about half to two thirds of employed adults holding their own plan fits both. Assigned by rank (larger employers and higher pay first), never a roll.

spread.citation: The Census Bureau's 2023 employment-based coverage rate and the KFF 2024 survey's mix of single and family coverage bound it; nothing measures the share directly.

healthMedicareAge.citation: Social Security Act sec. 1811 (42 U.S.C. 1395c): Medicare Part A eligibility begins at age 65.

traitWeightLifeDailyAct.citation: The trait weight of the life.daily-act decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightWorkAttendShift.citation: Salgado 2002, 'The Big Five personality dimensions and counterproductive behaviors' (International Journal of Selection and Assessment 10): 'none of the Big Five personality measures were found to be predictors of absenteeism'. The weight is the largest that keeps the odds of missing between the third leaning most toward missing and the third leaning least near a small single-decision effect (1.24 at 0.1 against an assumed 1.1 per standard deviation, scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts, Ely, Nevada, key 3223500, seed 7ae8589566f5, 14,008 shift weighings); at the general weight of 1 the ratio was 61, so temperament decided who missed work. Illness now decides most absences (workAbsenceIllnessWeight).

spread.citation: Odds ratios 1.16 to 1.72 between the thirds in the same calls; the study's null bounds it above.

traitWeightDrivesRespond.citation: The trait weight of the drives.respond decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightMacroRateVote.citation: The trait weight of the macro.rate-vote decision, fitted on a played year of Ely, Nevada (key 3223500, seed 7ae8589566f5) with 96 board votes by a finer sweep than scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts's 0.05 grid: 0.03 gives an odds ratio of 2.37 of moving the rate rather than holding between the thirds of votes leaning most toward moving and least, net of the same gap with personality off, against the target of 2.24 (the default personality-behavior study scaled for a single occasion to r = .2); personality turns about 5 of 100 votes. The module pulls (macroRatePullWeight) are large, so the fit is narrow. The board's hand-picked patience and risk traits (macroSmoothingPerPatience, macroMoveSizeCostPerRisk) were removed so personality enters the vote once, here.
traitWeightMacroRateVote.estimatedFrom: default.personality-behavior in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, scaled from average-level to a single occasion.

spread.citation: Weight at r = .1 and r = .3 of the single-occasion range (half and one and a half times the r = .2 weight).

traitWeightBusinessOwnerDraw.citation: The trait weight of the business.owner-draw decision, at the general traitWeight (1): no study of owners' draws by personality gives a number, so by the pool item's rule this decision keeps the general weight, with its gap row in data/content/trait-decision-gaps.json. An owner weighs the business's cash against a month of everything it pays out before drawing.

spread.reason: No study gives this decision a size; the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightBusinessOpenLocation.citation: The trait weight of the business.open-location decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightBusinessFound.citation: Zhao and Seibert 2006, The Big Five personality dimensions and entrepreneurial status (Journal of Applied Psychology 91(2)): multiple R .37 across the five traits, an odds ratio of 4.83 between the thirds. Weight set with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on played years of Holualoa, Hawaii (place key 1515700, seed 6f7794a4906f, 3,097 calls: weight 0.4, odds ratio 5.3), Peacham, Vermont (place key 5054325, seed 58e683537f9b, 10,373 calls: weight 0.3, odds ratio 5.0) and a third town (place key 2371780, seed c08fca61fc5c, 9,710 calls: weight 1.25, odds ratio 5.0), where many founders' cases are positive before personality; 0.6 sits between them. Full people take this weight on the chooser's arithmetic; the wider population keeps businessCountedFound's weight of 2.04 on its summed pull.

spread.citation: The three towns' fits; Zhao, Seibert and Lumpkin 2010 give R .36.

traitWeightJobsReviewWorker.citation: The trait weight of the jobs.review-worker decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightJobsValueWorker.citation: Barrick and Mount 1991 (Personnel Psychology 44(1), Table 2): conscientiousness correlates 0.22 with job performance. Sized so a business's valuation of a worker (years of tenure, or of experience when hiring, plus this term) correlates 0.22 with the worker's lean toward diligence: weight = 0.22 / sqrt(1 - 0.22^2) x the spread of real tenure / the spread of the lean within a firm. Real tenure spread 5.6 years: an exponential with the BLS median of 3.9 years (Employee Tenure in 2024, jobsTypicalTenureYears). Lean spread within a firm 0.29, the mean of three drawn places (Puapua, American Samoa, seed 5e38743ba0d3: 0.254; Melville, Rhode Island, seed f3c0bd5cabcd: 0.270; Middleborough Center, Massachusetts, seed 2c719d0f46f8: 0.341). Sized against real tenure, not the played world's, because the opening records no start date for anyone's job (src/core2/deep-past.ts:599), so tenure within a firm spans about five days at the start.

spread.unit: years of tenure or experience at full lean
spread.citation: Tenure spread 4.5 to 8 years (the exponential understates the long tail of BLS tenure) against a lean spread of 0.25 to 0.34 across the three places.

traitWeightJobsStartLooking.citation: The trait weight of the jobs.start-looking decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

traitWeightJobsApply.citation: The trait weight of the jobs.apply decision, at the general traitWeight (1): Kanfer, Wanberg and Kantrowitz 2001 (Journal of Applied Psychology 86(5)) report job search behavior's population correlations with its antecedents only as a range in the abstract (-.15 to .46), with no per-trait number retrieved, so by the pool item's rule this decision keeps the general weight, with its gap row in data/content/trait-decision-gaps.json. A seeker's push to apply eases with the weeks looked.

spread.reason: No study gives this decision a size; the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightHousingBuyHome.citation: The trait weight of the housing.buy-home decision: the general traitWeight (1). No study of personality and becoming a homeowner was found, and the fits with an assumed 1.2 per standard deviation disagree (Holualoa, Hawaii: 2.05 on 3 buyers; Peacham, Vermont: none reachable on 1; place key 2371780: 0.1, where the nearest households sit within a point of buying and odds are 11 at weight 1), so no weight is claimed from them.

spread.reason: Three drawn towns fit 0.1, 2.05 and none: a year holds one to sixteen households near enough to buy to be tipped, too few to fit.

traitWeightCreditBorrow.citation: Brown and Taylor 2014, Household finances and the 'Big Five' personality traits (Journal of Economic Psychology 45), Table 3 singles, probability of holding unsecured debt per standard deviation: conscientiousness -3.37 points, openness +3.35, extraversion +3.07 (base rate 0.4847), the strongest an odds ratio of 1.34 between the thirds. Weight set with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on played years of Holualoa, Hawaii (place key 1515700, seed 6f7794a4906f, 10,357 calls: weight 1.15, odds ratio 1.34) and Peacham, Vermont (place key 5054325, seed 58e683537f9b, 5,491 calls: weight 1.2, odds ratio 1.34). A stock of debt held is the nearest published proxy for the chance of taking it on.

spread.citation: Weights 1.0 to 1.4 give odds ratios of 1.29 to 1.40 between the thirds in the same calls; the study's interval for conscientiousness is -6.0 to -0.7 points.

traitWeightCandidacyRun.citation: van de Wardt, Bundi, Loewen, Rasmussen, Sheffer and Varone (2026), Too honest and humble to run for office?, European Journal of Political Research 65, having run for office, honesty-humility -0.03 per interquartile range: target odds ratio 1.21 between thirds. The chooser's trait term is the only place personality enters. Only newcomers weigh running: a serving incumbent weighs standing again (voting.stand-again). Running is rare among newcomers, so at the real share the few who run are those temperament tips over the line; the study's outcome (ever having run for office) has a base rate of a few percent, so the odds are read with every reason total moved so one in twenty would run. Fitted on 14,430 newcomers' decisions in the election-window years of four places drawn from all 56 (seeds e6cc8ea3d8b7, a3367c5b3f9c, fc53ee5340e9 and fd6b432aad56, scripts/traits/trait-wiring-audit.ts with TRAIT_AUDIT_ELECTION=1): the places fit alone at 0.15 to 0.22 and pooled at 0.23; 0.2 reaches 1.21 to 1.35 in them. Before incumbents left this choice it was fitted at 0.91 with their nearly certain yes in the sample.

spread.citation: The places' own fits at a one-in-twenty share, with Secretary, Maryland and Halaula, Hawaii (from the campaigns trait test at 0.91) at 0.12 and 0.11.

traitWeightSpeechRetell.citation: The trait weight of the speech.retell decision, fitted with the retelling case (speechKeepPull and the two engagement weights in src/core2/data/speech/parameters.json; traits-retell-circumstances) to Hibbing, Ritchie and Anderson 2011 (Political Behavior 33(4):601-624, Table 2, family discussion): conscientiousness 0.63 on the ordered log-odds of talking local politics with family over the trait's full range (SD 0.29), odds ratio 1.49 between the thirds. Read as crossed net odds (every weighing's case against every listener's lean, top third against bottom third) over 22,461 weighings in four drawn towns' played years, it gives 1.50 pooled and 1.42 to 1.91 by town.

spread.citation: The weights at which the pooled crossed net odds reach the study's interval, 1.2 to 2.4 (coefficient 0.63 plus or minus 1.96 standard errors of 0.28, scaled the same way), at this case.

traitWeightContractsAward.citation: The trait weight of the contracts.award decision: how far a member's traits move weight between price and the tie to a firm's owner (at full lean the price weight falls by this share and the tie weight rises by it). Replaces contractTraitWeight of 0.5. Not a two-way outcome, so scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts cannot fit it.

spread.citation: Weight at r = .1 and r = .3 of the single-occasion range (half and one and a half times the r = .2 weight).

traitWeightCorruptionOffer.citation: The trait weight of the corruption.offer decision, against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json (Pletzer, Bentvelzen, Oostrom and de Vries 2019, Journal of Vocational Behavior 112:369-383: honesty-humility against workplace deviance, corrected rho -0.482). Fitted Oct 24, 2026 on the offers play actually weighs: 16,228 asks kept by the trait audit in eleven played years of buildBenchWorld (Parkway, Missouri; Peacham, Vermont; Holualoa, Hawaii twice; Ilwaco, Washington; New Preston, Connecticut; Ora, Indiana; Arbela, Missouri; Jerry City, Ohio; New Britain, Connecticut; and the money branch's Peacham), each ask's favor, tie and reputation read from its kept case, with temperament carried by the shared chooser's trait term at traitWeightCorruptionOffer. Offers come from a town's lobbyists and bidding owners, not its adults at large, so a fit over every adult at one fixed favor would put the line where only money pressure reaches and no well-off lobbyist would ever offer. Fitted with corruptionHonestPull (3): 6.9 percent of asks offered, ratio between the thirds 7.8 against 11.0. It replaces the offer's own temperament term (corruptionTraitWeight, 1 on a lean scaled to -1 to 1), which the chooser's trait term had doubled.

spread.citation: Measured on the same 16,228 asks at the fitted pull: from 1 to 2.25 the rate stays 6.9 to 7.4 percent and the ratio 7.5 to 7.8; at 2.5 and above the most honest third never offers.

traitWeightCorruptionTake.citation: The trait weight of the corruption.take decision. Calibrated Oct 24, 2026 against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json (Pletzer, Bentvelzen, Oostrom and de Vries 2019, Journal of Vocational Behavior 112:369-383: honesty-humility against workplace deviance, corrected rho -0.482): on the adults of fourteen drawn towns (run seed fit1, label take-calibration) and checked on fourteen more (check2), the weight at which the third leaning most toward corruption takes as many times as often as the third leaning least as the latent model gives at the rate the towns show. Fitted with corruptionNeedWeight (0.5), corruptionPressureWeight (5.5) and corruptionTakeHonestPull (4.65): 6.3 percent take a $2,000 bribe from someone with a tie of 0.3, ratio 9.9 against 11.6 (check towns 7.2 percent, 11.8 against 10.7).

spread.citation: Measured on both sets of fourteen towns at the fitted reasons and pull: at 2.0 the fit towns' ratio between thirds is 0.66 of the latent model's and at 2.4 the check towns' is 1.54 of it; at 2.2 both sets are within a factor of 1.2.

traitWeightBusinessCountedFound.citation: Zhao and Seibert 2006 (Journal of Applied Psychology 91(2)): multiple R .37. Counted adults' founding pull is a logistic of their reasons; weight is ln(4.83) divided by 0.772, the mean lean gap between the thirds (place key 3223500, seed 7ae8589566f5), so the odds ratio between the thirds is the study's 4.83.

spread.citation: Zhao, Seibert and Lumpkin 2010 give R .36; the weight range gives odds ratios of 3 to 7.5 between the thirds.

traitWeightRetirementClaimAge.citation: Greenberg, Hershfield, Shu and Spiller 2018 (working paper, 20th Annual Joint Meeting of the Retirement Research Consortium), Table 2: intended Social Security claiming age rises 0.218 years per standard deviation of openness and 0.211 of agreeableness (standardized beta 0.078 and 0.075 on the 2.8-year spread of intended ages); the thirds of a trait sit 2.18 standard deviations apart, so 0.475 years. scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts cannot fit it: the case for waiting past the full retirement age clusters at one score, so the odds ratio is 1 up to a weight of 0.12 and over 3,000 at 0.15. Weight fitted directly: 0.475 years divided by claimTraitPullYears (4) times the mean lean gap between the thirds of those weighed (1.08 in Holualoa, Hawaii, place key 1515700, seed 6f7794a4906f, 5,574 calls; 0.71 in Peacham, Vermont, place key 5054325, seed 58e683537f9b, 2,131 calls), 0.11 and 0.17, set at the pooled 0.12.

spread.citation: The study's standard error (0.047 years for openness) gives 0.13 to 0.31 years per standard deviation, which at these lean gaps is a weight of 0.07 to 0.17.

traitWeightBringItUpBlame.citation: The trait weight of the bring-it-up.blame decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

traitWeightConversationBelieveClaim.citation: Sindermann, Schmitt, Rozgonjuk, Elhai and Montag 2021, The evaluation of fake and true news: on the role of intelligence, personality, interpersonal trust, ideological attitudes, and news consumption, Heliyon 7(3): extraversion correlates 0.09 with the number of 16 fake headlines a person judged true (N = 530 German adults; row conversation.believe-claim in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, a proxy: headlines, not a told claim). Carried to the thirds of hearers leaning most and least toward believing, that is a log odds gap of 0.357 (odds ratio 1.43). Goreis and Voracek 2019 (conspiracy belief, all five traits within 0.03 of zero) and the same paper's agreeableness (-0.03) say the pull is small. Weight found with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on a played year of each of two places drawn from all 56 (Halfway, Missouri, place key 2929962, seed 3e9ed70a5fb7, election window, 10,453 calls: 0.17; Marblehead, Ohio, place key 3947502, seed 7772ab1c8196, 13,123 calls: 0.20; stories told at a contact, speeches retold at home), taken as 0.18, which reaches 1.4 in both. The case it weighs against is the teller's closeness and the claim's fit with the hearer's views (believeClosenessWeight, believeFitWeight), so a doubter still believes a trusted friend.

spread.citation: Weight scales with the correlation: the study's 95% interval for extraversion is 0.005 to 0.174 (0.09 gives 0.18).
