traitWeightMovesMoveAway.citation: Jokela 2009, Personality predicts migration within and between U.S. states (Journal of Research in Personality 43(1)): openness, odds ratio 1.19 per standard deviation between states over 7 to 11 years. Moves are a pull multiplied by e to the net of pushes and holds, so the weight is ln(1.19^2.18) divided by 1.036, the mean lean gap between the third of counted adults leaning most toward moving and the third leaning least (place key 3223500, seed 7ae8589566f5): an odds ratio of 1.46 between the thirds.

spread.citation: Jokela's interval for openness, 1.04 to 1.36 per standard deviation, gives weights 0.08 to 0.65.

hardshipWeightMovesMoveAway.citation: Huttunen, Moen and Salvanes 2018, Job loss and regional mobility (Journal of Labor Economics 36(2); IZA DP 8780, Table 2 and p. 5): job displacement raises the probability of moving to a new region within two years by 0.6 percentage points for men (2% base) and 0.7 for women, about 30 percent, an odds ratio of 1.31 and 1.34. How much a lost job or a lost home speeds a person's pull to leave, per unit of the stress it left them, on the log scale the holds and pushes are added on (moves.ts pushesOf). The study sets only the mean effect of a job loss; the layoff stress it is divided by is the model's, not the study's. The studies of personality and moving (Jokela 2009) find no neuroticism effect, so the temperament in this term comes only from how hard the person is hit.
hardshipWeightMovesMoveAway.estimatedFrom: ln(1.325), the mean log odds ratio of the two sexes, 0.284, divided by the average layoff's stress 0.47. A layoff for a person of average temperament raises stress by 0.47 (47 of 100 Holmes and Rahe units, srrsFiredAtWork over srrsMaximumUnits, times lifeEventStressScale 1, with no closeness to themselves), so a weight is the study's log odds ratio divided by 0.47: the study's effect for the average layoff, and more or less for a person hit harder or softer (emotion.ts scales the impulse by their traits, Bolger and Schilling 1991). If lifeEventStressScale is recalibrated, divide these again.

spread.unit: log hazard of leaving per unit of stress
spread.citation: Women's interval in Table 2, 0.007 with standard error 0.001 on a 2.10% base: odds ratios 1.25 to 1.44, log 0.22 to 0.36, over 0.47.

hardshipWeightJobsBenefitsFileClaim.citation: Whittaker, Der, Cook and Saunders 2010, Predicting which people with psychosocial distress are at risk of becoming dependent on state benefits (BMJ 341:c3838): GHQ-12 psychological distress caseness rose before people started claiming incapacity benefit, odds ratio 1.6 (95% CI 1.3 to 1.9) from two years before. No study of stress and filing for unemployment insurance was found; this is the closest published size for how much distress raises claiming a state benefit, from a British panel of a disability benefit, so it names the direction (stress pulls toward claiming) and a size, not a measured effect on this filing. How much the stress a layoff left pulls an eligible worker toward filing, in the same score as the base and the traits' lean (jobs-benefits.ts fileClaim).
hardshipWeightJobsBenefitsFileClaim.estimatedFrom: ln(1.6), 0.47, for the average layoff's stress 0.47. A layoff for a person of average temperament raises stress by 0.47 (47 of 100 Holmes and Rahe units, srrsFiredAtWork over srrsMaximumUnits, times lifeEventStressScale 1, with no closeness to themselves), so a weight is the study's log odds ratio divided by 0.47: the study's effect for the average layoff, and more or less for a person hit harder or softer (emotion.ts scales the impulse by their traits, Bolger and Schilling 1991). If lifeEventStressScale is recalibrated, divide these again.

spread.citation: The study's interval, odds ratios 1.3 to 1.9, log 0.26 to 0.64, over 0.47.

hardshipWeightCreditBorrow.citation: Sullivan 2008, Borrowing during unemployment: unsecured debt as a safety net (Journal of Human Resources 43(2)): households with some assets that lose earnings to unemployment borrow, raising unsecured debt by more than 11 cents per dollar lost, while the poorest and the wealthy do not. The study gives an amount, not odds, so it sets the direction (a hardship pulls toward borrowing) and the size comes from the two studies that convert: the mean of the move weight's and the claim weight's log odds, 0.28 and 0.47. How much the stress a layoff, an eviction or a missed payment left pulls a household with a shortfall toward asking for a loan (credit.ts personalBorrowingDecision), in the same score as the baseline, need and cost.
hardshipWeightCreditBorrow.estimatedFrom: The mean of ln(1.325) and ln(1.6), 0.377, over the average layoff's stress 0.47. A layoff for a person of average temperament raises stress by 0.47 (47 of 100 Holmes and Rahe units, srrsFiredAtWork over srrsMaximumUnits, times lifeEventStressScale 1, with no closeness to themselves), so a weight is the study's log odds ratio divided by 0.47: the study's effect for the average layoff, and more or less for a person hit harder or softer (emotion.ts scales the impulse by their traits, Bolger and Schilling 1991). If lifeEventStressScale is recalibrated, divide these again.

spread.citation: The move weight (0.6) and the claim weight (1.0) it averages.

traitWeightVotingTurnout.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson 2010, Personality and Civic Engagement: An Integrative Framework for the Study of Trait Effects on Political Behavior, American Political Science Review 104(1): openness to experience raises the log odds of reporting having voted by 1.26 across the trait's full 0-to-1 range (2006 CES, N about 1,060), which Mondak et al. call among the largest effects in their Table 2. Carried to the thirds of people leaning most and least toward voting, that is a log odds gap of 0.604 (odds ratio 1.83). Weight found by measuring the turnout propensity (turnoutReasons through the turnout logistic) of every adult over six drawn places (seeds c1, d1, d3, d12, c2, d2 with the label trait-wiring, buildBenchWorld, 60 days) at weights 0 to 1.2, net of the same gap at weight 0, and solving for 0.549: 0.716. The emotional-stability row (-1.42) is not used: its sign runs against the trait's lean and the authors flag it as inconsistent with earlier work. Rescaled Oct 24 by the trait's own standard deviation from the paper's Table 1 (0.22 of its full range, against the 0.2 first assumed), so the target and the weight both grow by 1.1: 0.716 became 0.79.

spread.citation: Weight scales with the coefficient: the study's 95% interval for the openness coefficient is 0.378 to 2.142.

traitWeightVotingBackIncumbent.citation: The trait weight of the voting.back-incumbent decision. Backing the incumbent adds the voter's lean toward keeping the known over trying someone new to the incumbent's appeal. The research row for it in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json gives no effect size, so the general traitWeight (1) stands until a study gives one.

spread.reason: No effect size found for this decision; until one is, the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightVotingExitPoll.citation: Kostadintcheva, Kuha and Sturgis 2025, Survey Experience and Nonresponse in an Online Probability Panel (arXiv 2505.03971), Table 3: conscientiousness -0.095 log odds of not responding per point of a 1-5 scale; "The least Conscientious panel members have a nonresponse probability of 21% compared to 15% for the most"), row voting.exit-poll in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, carried to the thirds as an odds ratio of 1.18. Fitted with the exit poll's case (exitPollBase, exitPollEngagementWeight, exitPollInterestWeight) on the named voters of three drawn race towns, Finklea, South Carolina (4525405, seed 100a9eddd8c1), Silver City, Nevada (3266800, 62fd4b12c74d) and Douglas, Nebraska (3113505, d6f5f50c5452): crossed net odds 1.18 pooled, 1.14 to 1.35 by town; temperament turns 3.6% of answers. At the general weight of 1 with a case of 0 the thirds ran at 35.

spread.citation: The conscientiousness standard deviation behind the target is assumed (0.15 to 0.25 of the scale's range), which moves the target from 1.13 to 1.23.

traitWeightVotingStandAgain.citation: van de Wardt, Bundi, Loewen, Rasmussen, Sheffer and Varone (2026), Too honest and humble to run for office?, European Journal of Political Research 65, having run for office, honesty-humility -0.03 per interquartile range, as the proxy for an incumbent standing again (no study of incumbents' decisions was found): target odds ratio 1.21 between thirds. Found by the cross-product method over the ages of Newfane VT's adults 30 to 85 with the age reason added to the decision, so that 82% stand (about 81% of local incumbents seek reelection). Reached 1.19.

spread.citation: Scaled linearly from the study's reported interval (or half to one and a half times where none is reported) to the weight.

traitWeightCampaignsVolunteer.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson (2010), Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), Table 2, worked for a party or candidate, openness logit 2.02 over the trait's full range (95% interval 0.57 to 3.47): target odds ratio 2.63 between thirds (2.41 before the rescale below). Found with the cross-product calibration of the played years of Newfane VT, Ute IA, Clifton KS and Cameron SC (seeds c1, d1, d3, d12, 365 days each, scripts/traits/trait-wiring-audit.ts): every kept reason total met with every kept trait lean, the weight at which the odds of the studied option between the top and bottom third of lean match the study's, with the volunteer threshold set at 1.0 (the largest the campaign calibration test's range of acquaintances who volunteer allows without losing the closest circle). Reached 2.42. Rescaled Oct 24 by the trait's own standard deviation from the paper's Table 1 (0.22 of its full range, against the 0.2 first assumed), so the target and the weight both grow by 1.1: 0.15 became 0.165.

spread.citation: Scaled linearly from the study's reported interval (or half to one and a half times where none is reported) to the weight.

traitWeightCampaignsDonate.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson (2010), Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), Table 2, contributed money, openness logit 1.25 (interval 0.41 to 2.09): target odds ratio 1.82 between thirds (1.72 before the rescale below). Found with the cross-product calibration of the played years of Newfane VT, Ute IA, Clifton KS and Cameron SC (seeds c1, d1, d3, d12, 365 days each, scripts/traits/trait-wiring-audit.ts): every kept reason total met with every kept trait lean, the weight at which the odds of the studied option between the top and bottom third of lean match the study's, with the threshold moved so the share who say yes is unchanged. Reached 1.72 on whether a person's reasons to give clear zero; no threshold moved because a gift grows with the reason. Rescaled Oct 24 by the trait's own standard deviation from the paper's Table 1 (0.22 of its full range, against the 0.2 first assumed), so the target and the weight both grow by 1.1: 0.065 became 0.0715.

spread.citation: Scaled linearly from the study's reported interval (or half to one and a half times where none is reported) to the weight.

traitWeightCampaignsEndorse.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson 2010, Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), Table 2 (rows campaigns.endorse in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json: openness and extraversion on having tried to convince people to vote for or against a candidate, a proxy for an endorsement), carried to the thirds as an odds ratio of 2.70. Fitted with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on played years (buildBenchWorld, every module, January 20, 2025 to January 20, 2026): Haledon, New Jersey (place key 3429070, seed fc8bf1311d0f) fits 0.2 on 1,053 calls and Kenvir, Kentucky (2142112, seed 32bb83941552) fits 0.1 on 62. At 0.15 Haledon's thirds reach 2.12, or 2.76 with every case crossed with every decider's lean; at the general weight of 1 they ran at 269.

spread.citation: The two towns' own fits.

traitWeightCampaignsOpenDoor.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson (2010), Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), contacted a member of Congress, extraversion 0.27 to 0.49 across its range (logit 0.92, SE 0.27), used as the citizen-side proxy for answering a stranger's knock: target odds ratio 1.66 between thirds (1.48 before the rescale below). Found with the cross-product calibration of the played years of Newfane VT, Ute IA, Clifton KS and Cameron SC (seeds c1, d1, d3, d12, 365 days each, scripts/traits/trait-wiring-audit.ts): every kept reason total met with every kept trait lean, the weight at which the odds of the studied option between the top and bottom third of lean match the study's, with the threshold moved so the share who say yes is unchanged. Reached 1.44. Rescaled Oct 24 by the trait's own standard deviation from the paper's Table 1 (0.26 of its full range, against the 0.2 first assumed), so the target and the weight both grow by 1.3: 0.085 became 0.1105.

spread.citation: Scaled linearly from the study's reported interval (or half to one and a half times where none is reported) to the weight.

traitWeightCampaignsRetell.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson (2010), Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), Table 2, tried to convince people how to vote, openness logit 2.07 (interval 1.40 to 2.74), as the proxy for telling family a campaign story (no study of retelling by personality was found): target ratio 2.70 between thirds (2.47 before the rescale below). A retelling's reach is 1 plus this weight times the lean, so the weight is the one at which the top third's mean reach is 2.45 times the bottom third's across the adults of Newfane VT (seed c1). The campaign's second-hand weight was lowered to keep the town's mean reach where it was. Rescaled Oct 24 by the trait's own standard deviation from the paper's Table 1 (0.22 of its full range, against the 0.2 first assumed), so the target grows by 1.1 (log odds 0.903 to 0.993). A retelling's reach is 1 plus the weight times the lean, so it does not scale exactly with the target; the weight is found again the same way on the adults of Newfane VT (seed c1): the top third's mean reach is 2.45 times the bottom's at 4.9 and 2.71 times at 5.8, against the new 2.70, and a plain 1.1 scale (5.39) would reach only 2.59. 4.9 became 5.8. That lifts the town's mean reach from 1.65 to 1.77 times, which the campaign's second-hand weight is set from. Found again Oct 27 (tests-campaign-traits-ratios-out-of-band-st-paul): the act-kind pull table (data/content/trait-act-pulls.json) was rebuilt after the Oct 24 weight, which left the lean of speaking out against staying quiet about five times wider, so at 5.8 the top third's reach was 21 to 29 times the bottom's in every one of six drawn towns (seed scratch:0 to scratch:5, adults at the opening). The weight at which the ratio is 2.70 is 1.09 to 1.17 in each of the six towns, 1.13 pooled. That lowers the town's mean reach to 1.23 times, and the campaign's second-hand weight is set again from it.

spread.citation: Scaled linearly from the study's reported interval (or half to one and a half times where none is reported) to the weight.

traitWeightCampaignsAnswerPoll.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson (2010), Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), contacted a member of Congress, extraversion (proxy for answering a pollster's call; no study of poll response by personality was found): target odds ratio 1.66 between thirds (1.48 before the rescale below). Found by the same cross-product method on the age reasons of every adult of Newfane VT (seed c1) met with their trait leans, with the threshold moved so the share who answer is unchanged. Reached 1.46. Rescaled Oct 24 by the trait's own standard deviation from the paper's Table 1 (0.26 of its full range, against the 0.2 first assumed), so the target and the weight both grow by 1.3: 0.095 became 0.1235. Found again Oct 27 (tests-campaign-traits-ratios-out-of-band-st-paul) by the same method on the adults of six drawn towns at the opening (seed scratch:0 to scratch:5): the act-kind pull table (data/content/trait-act-pulls.json) was rebuilt after the Oct 24 weight, so at 0.1235 the odds ratio was 3.3 to 5.1 against 1.66; the weight that reaches 1.66 is 0.0082 to 0.0107 in each town, 0.0092 in the middle.

spread.citation: Scaled linearly from the study's reported interval (or half to one and a half times where none is reported) to the weight.

traitWeightCampaignsRivalHours.citation: The trait weight of the campaigns.rival-hours decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightPartiesJoin.citation: Linkov 2020, Political party membership and personality characteristics in the Czech Republic (2005), E-psychologie 14(2): members of eight Czech parties (194, NEO-FFI) scored higher on extraversion than the population, a standardized difference of 0.346 that the research helper turned into an odds ratio of 1.41 per standard deviation (row parties.join in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json: derived from the printed party means, not printed as one number, and a proxy: party membership in another country, 2005). Carried to the thirds of tied people leaning most and least toward joining (2.18 standard deviations apart), that is a log odds gap of 0.748 (odds ratio 2.11). Weight found with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on a played year of Marblehead, Ohio (place key 3947502, seed 7772ab1c8196, 66 calls; Halfway, Missouri weighed only 13): 0.75 reaches 3.1, the nearest step to 2.1 because the case (the tie to the party) sorts people into a few lumps. The case it weighs against is partiesJoinBase for a person already tied to a party.

spread.citation: Weight scales with the log odds ratio: the helper's interval for extraversion is 1.21 to 1.65 per standard deviation (1.41 gives 0.75).

traitWeightPartiesAttend.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson 2010, Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), Table 2: extraversion raises the log odds of having attended political meetings or election rallies by 1.65 across the trait's full 0-to-1 range (2006 CES, N about 1,066; row parties.attend in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, a proxy: the survey does not separate a party's own meeting). Carried to the thirds of members leaning most and least toward attending with the trait's own standard deviation from their Table 1 (0.26 of its range), that is a log odds gap of 0.935 (odds ratio 2.55; Gerber et al. 2011's campaign-rally coefficient 1.049 gives 1.94). Weight found with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on one played election-window year of Halfway, Missouri (place key 2929962, seed 3e9ed70a5fb7, 5,248 calls, party meetings and candidate events together since both read this decision): 0.55 reaches 2.58. The case it weighs against is the member's free time and distance from the meeting (partyMeetingFreeTimeWeight, partyMeetingDistanceWeight), so no temperament decides alone.

spread.citation: Weight scales with the coefficient: the study's 95% interval for the Mondak extraversion coefficient is 0.67 to 2.63 (1.65 gives 0.55).

traitWeightStaffHire.citation: Kardaslar, Kritikos and Menkhoff 2026, Personality Traits of Entrepreneurs and the Size of Their Firms, DIW Discussion Paper 2173, Table 6: openness changes the odds of running a business alone rather than with at least one employee by a factor of 0.776 per standard deviation (SOEP 2019, 2,473 entrepreneurs; row staff.hire in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, a proxy: a first employee, not an official's staff). Carried to the thirds, an odds ratio of 1.74. Fitted by crossing every case kept in a played year with every decider's lean, so the thirds of deciders face the same cases (scripts/traits/trait-wiring-matrix.ts, crossedNetOddsRatio): a town has only 2 to 10 officials handling cases, so the plain thirds rest on one to three people each. At 0.2, where office budgets differ, Blakely, Georgia (1308536, a458468e363e) reaches 2.17 over 35 officials; where every office can afford an aide, as in Stockbridge, Georgia (1373704, bde29897f271), temperament turns none (1.00), the gap row's subject (gov-official-staff-allowance-by-office).

spread.citation: The crossed fit's neighbors in Blakely: 0.15 gives 1.71 and 0.3 gives 4.11.

traitWeightInterestGroupsMemberJoin.citation: Bekkers 2005, Participation in Voluntary Associations: Relations with Resources, Personality, and Political Values, Political Psychology 26(3), model 1: per standard deviation of agreeableness the odds of belonging to a (quasi-)political association (parties, unions, professional, religious and similar groups) against none fall to 0.79 (conscientiousness 0.81, extraversion 1.14; row interest-groups.member-join in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, a proxy: the category pools seven kinds of organization and the paper prints no interval). Carried to the thirds of residents leaning most and least toward joining (2.18 standard deviations apart), that is a log odds gap of 0.514 (odds ratio 1.67). Weight found with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on one played election-window year of Halfway, Missouri (place key 2929962, seed 3e9ed70a5fb7, 3,172 calls): 0.115 reaches 1.65. The case it weighs against is how hard the question pulls the resident plus how strongly the group's members already draw them in (groupDrawWeight), against the bar.

spread.citation: The paper prints no interval; the other two traits' odds ratios per standard deviation (0.81 and 1.14) fit weights of 0.10 and 0.08, and its model 2 with resources controlled (agreeableness 0.90) fits 0.05.

traitWeightInterestGroupsEmployerJoin.citation: The trait weight of the interest-groups.employer-join decision. An owner joins an employers' association when what the bill costs the firm against the dues plus their lean toward joining is above zero. The research row for it in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json gives no effect size, so the general traitWeight (1) stands until a study gives one.

spread.reason: No effect size found for this decision; until one is, the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightInterestGroupsLobbyist.citation: Gerber, Huber, Doherty, Dowling, Raso and Ha 2011, Personality Traits and Participation in Political Processes, Journal of Politics 73(3), on-line appendix Table A12a: extraversion raises the log odds of having spoken at a local public meeting by 0.978 across the trait's full 0-to-1 range (CT Survey 2008, N = 1,924; row interest-groups.lobbyist in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, a proxy: no study of who serves as a group's spokesperson was found). Carried to the thirds of members leaning most and least toward serving with the survey's own standard deviation (0.29), that is a log odds gap of 0.618 (odds ratio 1.86). Weight found with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on one played election-window year of Halfway, Missouri (place key 2929962, seed 3e9ed70a5fb7, 500 calls): the stake is a few lumps, so the fit steps from 1.2 at 0.25 to 3.0 at 0.3, and 0.3 is kept: it reaches 3.0 against the target 1.86 (a factor of 1.6) in Halfway and 5.0 (a factor of 2.7) in Marblehead, Ohio (place key 3947502, seed 7772ab1c8196, 1,059 calls), where trait-calibrate finds no step that reaches the study.

spread.citation: Weight scales with the coefficient: the study's 95% interval for the extraversion coefficient is 0.502 to 1.454 (0.978 gives 0.3).

traitWeightOfficesAcceptAppointment.citation: The trait weight of the offices.accept-appointment decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightLegislatureMemberPosition.citation: The trait weight of the legislature.member-position decision, set by the party discipline a member's position must keep once officials carry a level on every trait (pool item officials-carry-every-trait). With every trait, a member's taste for change is a standing lean on every bill, so at 0.6 (fitted to the generic single-occasion personality target of 2.24) the two independent senators in the world drawn from seed 3e556e7e162eca8baf7052af5494da02 (Fenwick, West Virginia) voted with their caucus on 55 of 90 party votes, against about 90% for the real independents (Voteview, the caucus weight's check). At 0.1 the independents of four drawn worlds vote with their caucus on 0.80, 0.98, 0.90 and 0.95 of party votes (mean 0.91; seeds 3e556e7e162eca8baf7052af5494da02, caucusA1, caucusB2, caucusC3), and party members' pooled unity on party-splitting votes is 0.943 over four drawn places (src/core2/party-loyalty.test.ts, seed loyalty01, against its 0.85 to 0.98 band from CQ Vote Studies). The generic target is not used here: a legislator's roll call is dominated by party, and no study found gives personality's size per roll call.
traitWeightLegislatureMemberPosition.estimatedFrom: The independents' caucus unity (about 90%, Voteview 118th to 119th Congress, as the officials roster's caucus weight cites) and party unity (about 90%, CQ Vote Studies, the party-loyalty band), read in drawn worlds at weights 0.05 to 0.6.

spread.citation: At 0.15 the Fenwick world's independents vote with their caucus on 70 of 92 party votes (0.76) and the four worlds' mean is 0.89; at 0.05, 0.79 and 0.91.

traitWeightLegislatureHoldHearing.citation: The trait weight of the legislature.hold-hearing decision, found with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on two played years pooled, after officials carry a level on every trait (pool item officials-carry-every-trait): Pomona, New Jersey (key 3460030, seed 7628f7fcf9e0) and the place drawn from seed f9a9cd8421fe (key 2684360): 0.65 gives an odds ratio of 2.32 of holding the hearing between the thirds of 172 chair decisions, against the target of 2.24. The places fit alone at 0.1 (77 decisions) and 1.0 (95). It was 1.35 when fitted in Ely, Nevada on 78 decisions while officials carried nine faint traits.
traitWeightLegislatureHoldHearing.estimatedFrom: default.personality-behavior in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, scaled from average-level to a single occasion; replaces the hand-set traitDecisionWeight of 0.5.

spread.citation: The two places' own fits, each on fewer than 100 chair decisions.

traitWeightLegislatureSignOrVeto.citation: The trait weight of the legislature.sign-or-veto decision, found with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on two played years pooled, after officials carry a level on every trait (pool item officials-carry-every-trait): Pomona, New Jersey (key 3460030, seed 7628f7fcf9e0) and the place drawn from seed f9a9cd8421fe (key 2684360): the 59 desk decisions saturate (the odds ratio between the thirds is 78 at weight 1), and 0.1 comes closest to the target of 2.24 (2.62). The second place alone fits 0.3 on 31 decisions.
traitWeightLegislatureSignOrVeto.estimatedFrom: traitWeightLegislatureMemberPosition (0.2), calibrated on 10,336 calls; replaces the hand-set traitDecisionWeight of 0.5.

spread.citation: The pooled and the second place's fits.

traitWeightLegislatureBudgetPriorities.citation: The trait weight of the legislature.budget-priorities decision: how far an executive's temperament scales how much of the budget they move (a multiplier of 1 plus the weight times the lean, so a lean of 1 moves half again as much). Not a two-way outcome, so scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts cannot fit it; carries the 0.5 the site used as traitDecisionWeight, with a spread of half to one and a half of that.

spread.citation: Weight at r = .1 and r = .3 of the single-occasion range (half and one and a half times the r = .2 weight).

traitWeightWorldLegislatingBringAgenda.citation: The trait weight of the world-legislating.bring-agenda decision, found with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on a played year of Ely, Nevada (key 3223500, seed 7ae8589566f5): 0.15 gives an odds ratio of 2.31 of filing a change between the thirds of 4,583 filing decisions, against the target of 2.24 (the default personality-behavior study scaled for a single occasion to r = .2).
traitWeightWorldLegislatingBringAgenda.estimatedFrom: default.personality-behavior in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, scaled from average-level to a single occasion; replaces the hand-set traitDecisionWeight of 0.5.

spread.citation: Weight at r = .1 and r = .3 of the single-occasion range (half and one and a half times the r = .2 weight).

traitWeightConstituentCasesBringCase.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson 2010, Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), Table 2: extraversion raises the log odds of having contacted a House member or senator by 0.92 across the trait's range (row constituent-cases.bring-case in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, a proxy: any contact), a log odds gap of 0.52 between thirds (odds ratio 1.68). A resident's case carries the problem's severity and their interest in politics against the effort. Fitted by crossing every case kept in a played year with every decider's lean, so the thirds of deciders face the same cases (scripts/traits/trait-wiring-matrix.ts, crossedNetOddsRatio): a town has only 2 to 10 officials handling cases, so the plain thirds rest on one to three people each. At 0.045, one played year each, every module: Blakely, Georgia (place key 1308536, seed a458468e363e) 1.62 over 366 residents; Stockbridge, Georgia (1373704, bde29897f271) 2.87 over 845.

spread.citation: The crossed fit's neighbors in the same years: 0.03 gives 1.36 to 2.16 and 0.06 about 1.9 to 3.6.

traitWeightConstituentCasesHandleCase.citation: Barrick and Mount 1991, The Big Five personality dimensions and job performance, Personnel Psychology 44(1): conscientiousness correlates about 0.22 with job performance, an odds ratio of 2.44 between thirds (row constituent-cases.handle-case in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json, a proxy: an official's diligence with a case as job performance). The official weighs the case's own circumstances (severity, closeness to the resident, the office's open load); nearly every case is helped, so a small weight already turns the few that sit near the line. Fitted by crossing every case kept in a played year with every decider's lean, so the thirds of deciders face the same cases (scripts/traits/trait-wiring-matrix.ts, crossedNetOddsRatio): a town has only 2 to 10 officials handling cases, so the plain thirds rest on one to three people each. At 0.02, one played year each, every module: Blakely, Georgia (1308536, a458468e363e) 3.02 over 10 officials; Stockbridge, Georgia (1373704, bde29897f271) 2.51 over 8.

spread.citation: The crossed fit's neighbors: 0.01 gives about 1 to 1.9 and 0.025 about 5, where the cases near the line all turn.

traitWeightStaffFollowThrough.citation: Barrick and Mount 1991 (as for constituent-cases.handle-case): conscientiousness and job performance, an odds ratio of 2.44 between thirds (row staff.follow-through in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json). A staffer weighs their work quality against the follow-through bar and the office's open load. Fitted by crossing every case kept in a played year with every decider's lean, so the thirds of deciders face the same cases (scripts/traits/trait-wiring-matrix.ts, crossedNetOddsRatio): a town has only 2 to 10 officials handling cases, so the plain thirds rest on one to three people each. At 0.2, one played year each, every module: Blakely, Georgia (1308536, a458468e363e) 1.38 over 10 staffers; Stockbridge, Georgia (1373704, bde29897f271) 2.95 over 10.

spread.citation: The crossed fit's neighbors: 0.15 gives 1.07 to 2.76 and 0.25 gives 1.92 to 3.42.

traitWeightJobsBenefitsFileClaim.citation: The trait weight of the jobs-benefits.file-claim decision, at the general traitWeight (1). Vella, Richiardi and van de Ven 2025 give an odds ratio of 1.32 between the thirds (row jobs-benefits.file-claim in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json), but no weight reaches it: within a town the benefit replaces the same share of pay for nearly every worker, so temperament and the layoff's stress (itself read through temperament) are the only reasons that vary, and the thirds' odds run 6 to 20 at any weight from 0.1 to 1.2 once take-up is near 0.73 (SG-TRAITS-file-claim-circumstances-tie).

spread.reason: No weight fits the study until the filing reads circumstances that vary between workers; until then, the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightNewsPassOn.citation: Lin, Wang and Sun 2024, How big five personality traits influence information sharing on social media: A meta analysis, PLOS ONE 19(6): extraversion has a pooled standardized beta of 0.05 on information sharing (27 studies, N=31,969). Carried to the thirds of people leaning most and least toward passing news on, that is a log rate gap of 0.198 (a rate ratio of 1.22). Stories passed at a contact are a rate, not a probability, so the gap is measured on the stories owed at a contact (storiesOwedAtContact), which grow as one plus the weight times the lean, by every adult over six drawn places (seeds c1, d1, d3, d12, c2, d2 with the label trait-wiring). Remeasured Oct 26, 2026: the thirds now sit 1.10 to 1.12 apart in lean (Newfane, Vermont; Ute, Iowa; Clifton, Kansas; Cameron, South Carolina; Frederiksted, U.S. Virgin Islands; Lockhart, Alabama), against about 0.71 when the weight was first found at 0.277, which then gave 0.30 in every town. The weight solving for 0.198 runs 0.178 to 0.187 across the six, mean 0.182. The agreeableness beta (-0.06) is not used: the lean toward telling is carried by extraversion and sociability.

spread.citation: The study reports no interval; the same sentence reports betas of 0.03 to 0.06 for the other traits, and solved the same way over the same six places those give weights of 0.108 and 0.219.

traitWeightPressFollowNews.citation: Sindermann, Schmitt and others 2021 (rows press.follow-news in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json): extraversion correlates 0.16 with the number of news sources a German adult follows (openness 0.12, neuroticism -0.09). A person's habit is their political engagement plus the weighted lean, and each kind of news (local paper, television, radio, and the national kinds) takes the top of each age band by habit at its researched share, so the weight is set so the lean correlates 0.16 with the number of kinds a person follows. Fitted by rebuilding the audiences at each weight over every adult of two played towns (buildBenchWorld, every module): Lookeba, Oklahoma (place key 4044000, seed f20e6549007c, 57 adults) reaches 0.16 at about 0.02 and Jagual, Puerto Rico (7237166, seed d29d296abf1f, 112 adults) at about 0.11; pooled, 0.08.

spread.citation: The two towns' own fits.

traitWeightPressAcceptInterview.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson (2010), Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), tried to convince people how to vote, openness logit 2.07 (interval 1.40 to 2.74), as the proxy for speaking to a reporter: target odds ratio 2.70 between thirds, with the trait's own spread from the paper's Table 1 (0.22 of its full range). Fitted on the interview asks of two played election-window years (Halfway, Missouri, seed 3e9ed70a5fb7; Marblehead, Ohio, seed 7772ab1c8196), every kept case (the base, the outlet's reach and the seat, src/core2/data/press/parameters.json) crossed with every candidate's lean: odds 3.06 and 3.48 between the thirds at 1.1. In small drawn towns whose residents are all named, where nearly every candidate is known to the whole town, 0.57 reaches the same odds.

spread.citation: Scaled from the study's interval for the coefficient, 1.40 to 2.74 around 2.07.

traitWeightPressDig.citation: The trait weight of the press.dig decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightPressShadeAnswer.citation: The trait weight of the press.shade-answer decision. Heck, Thielmann, Moshagen and Hilbig (2018), Judgment and Decision Making 13(4):356-371: honesty-humility lowers the odds of lying for gain, odds ratio 0.53 per standard deviation ("The results show a medium to large effect of HH (odds ratio = 0.53)"; "The odds ratio for a z-standardized predictor"), as the proxy for shading an answer about one's own vote toward the town: target log odds 1.38 between the top and bottom thirds (2.18 standard deviations apart). The gap between the vote and where the town stands is the only circumstance and the target is set on the latent-logit scale, as for press.accept-interview: the target divided by the gap between the top and bottom third's mean lean toward shading over owning (1.27 to 1.28, scaled and clamped as the formula reads it) across the adults of 16 towns drawn from all 56 places (seeds shadefit1 and shadefit2). Town by town the fitted weight runs 1.03 to 1.13 (measured across the 16 towns, separate from the study's own uncertainty).

spread.citation: The weight scales with the log odds ratio: the study's 95% Bayesian credibility interval for the odds ratio is 0.47 to 0.60 (Section 3.1: "HH resulted in a medium to large effect of OR = 0.53 with a 95% BCI of [0.47; 0.60]"; Table 2: 0.53, 2.5% 0.47, 97.5% 0.60).

traitWeightPressTip.citation: The trait weight of the press.tip decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightMeetingsTakePart.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson 2010, Personality and Civic Engagement: An Integrative Framework for the Study of Trait Effects on Political Behavior, American Political Science Review 104(1): extraversion raises the log odds of having attended a public meeting with a House member or senator by 1.92 across the trait's full range (2006 CES; the trait's spread is 0.26 of its range, Table 1), which Mondak et al. call among the largest effects in their Table 2. Carried to the thirds of people leaning most and least toward taking part, that is a log odds gap of 1.088 (odds ratio 2.97). Weight found in played years, on every meeting's whole pool of residents (each one's feeling about the question and their lean, and the room's size), so the room can be refilled at any weight: who took part at a bill's public comment and in a town hall's room, by thirds of lean over every resident weighed, net of the room filled with temperament left out. Refilled at 0.32, 0.285 and 0.26 in twenty drawn places' election windows on fresh random seeds (Oct 27, 2026, at #6143's head 99fc0b1579, one seed per place, each with its run seed, attempt and the different residents weighed): Jeromesville, Ohio (4565776ec6bbd777753e60793e3adb75d8170e85:meetings:0, 390 residents); Calumet, Oklahoma (4a3b742ed67a678280bb52c5e07946e6e056e99a:meetings:2, 388 residents); Loa, Utah (5b9f5133d4f09b48c17a1400ad9997c407f6a142:meetings:2, 386 residents); Grantsville, West Virginia (d85ba81c178988779216ba453c4d543af4d73826:meetings:0, 380 residents); Coopers Plains, New York (346297ca0c6347ebfe6283a726b7412fed002820:meetings:3, 359 residents); Richfield, Idaho (bf0c8cccea59d47b0486b8429ab231660fa1e2cf:meetings:0, 354 residents); Giltner, Nebraska (4171548db447be0cfb2f201f22f696e0cc6ad026:meetings:1, 335 residents); Pine Valley, Utah (290e684e1f4554f4ad97658260426b08a21bb8ce:meetings:4, 333 residents); Wyoming, Rhode Island (2e0a45586bc2a827a0ef4372ab71387d6e507c8c:meetings:0, 302 residents); Swan Valley, Idaho (2f234763e0a847d5c8cd10891133cf5d6b01b22e:meetings:0, 284 residents); Bruce Crossing, Michigan (80299d07892cb4e564190c33540ba3a9b18da828:meetings:0, 222 residents); Candlewood Lake Club, Connecticut (4f9c09e5328fcba61e895d18e33cd25308834fb3:meetings:1, 220 residents); Harrison, Idaho (22bb62bc23a274d0b1d405e6b0c7705d455c1077:meetings:1, 220 residents); Nikep, Maryland (32a42565139ff132b9992b2c0147d78c7875c620:meetings:2, 205 residents); Henry, Nebraska (6ac4606bddc97bbafb62c8157cf9ae99e1d60582:meetings:0, 141 residents); Garvin, Oklahoma (9cf6b1d5763b91a28c6b92e45d99332f2878e938:meetings:4, 138 residents); Leadore, Idaho (7bdcc2cf53d4d7f38de0cdacbbe82137ad6725d5:meetings:1, 75 residents); Whitney, Nebraska (5b9f5133d4f09b48c17a1400ad9997c407f6a142:meetings:1, 59 residents); Antelope Hills, Wyoming (c2ef691f6254c1bafe3eab93d9fd2b7522e5a6a1:meetings:0, 54 residents); Solen, North Dakota (7edd8f59102f8f866da350644620baf5e6ca3e0f:meetings:1, 50 residents). A refill matched the played run to within 0.08 in seven real runs at 0.285 and 0.26. In the 16 places with 100 or more different residents weighed the net log odds at 0.26 have geometric mean 1.077 against the study's 1.088 (0.52 to 2.04 singly; 1.410 at 0.32, 1.229 at 0.285), and all 20 together 0.961 (1.206 at 0.32). Antelope Hills and Whitney stay flat (0.31 and 0.35 at any weight below 0.4, and 0.306 and 0.329 at 0.26): their rooms of 40 fill from about 55 residents driven, the same people at every town hall, so temperament has almost nobody to turn away and the 418 and 1,068 weighings are 54 and 59 different residents; they would need weights of 0.445 and 0.785 to reach 1.088, which put 8 of the first 17 places over the band at 0.45. One town's thirds still swing from about 0.5 to 2.4 around the study's 1.088, nearly the width of the test's band, which is why the meetings test pools two towns. A fifth to a third of residents feel as strongly as anyone can about a question, and among them temperament alone sets who fills the room, which is why the weight sits below the 0.5 that two towns' audit years first gave (Halfway, Missouri and Marblehead, Ohio: net odds 2.01 and 4.16 at 0.5, 1.62 and 2.95 at 0.35).

spread.citation: The 10th to 90th percentile (0.152 to 0.447) of the weights at which each of the twenty drawn places' own net first reaches the study's 1.088 (the places' weights ran 0.06 to 0.785, median 0.278); the study's own 95% interval for the extraversion coefficient, 1.195 to 2.645, scales to 0.16 to 0.36 at this weight.

traitWeightSchoolAttend.citation: The trait weight of the school.attend decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightJusticeReport.citation: Weight on the person's traits (speaking out and following the rules against staying quiet) when deciding to report a bribe they refused or were told of; whistleblowing tracks conscientiousness and moral courage (Bjorkelo, Einarsen and Matthiesen 2010). Carried from the former reportTraitWeight.

spread.citation: The former parameter's spread, carried with it.

traitWeightJusticeProsecute.citation: Weight on a prosecutor's own traits (confronting against playing safe) when deciding whether a case is worth opening and charging; half the reporter's: the office's standards narrow a prosecutor's own temperament. Carried from the former prosecutorTraitWeight.

spread.citation: The former parameter's spread, carried with it.

traitWeightJusticePlea.citation: Weight on the defendant's traits (conceding against confronting) when weighing a plea against trial; smaller than the case's own strength, since about 90% of federal convictions came by plea (Bureau of Justice Statistics, Federal Justice Statistics 2022). Carried from the former pleaTraitWeight.

spread.citation: The former parameter's spread, carried with it.

traitWeightMeetingsHoldTownHall.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson 2010, Personality and Civic Engagement: An Integrative Framework for the Study of Trait Effects on Political Behavior, American Political Science Review 104(1): extraversion raises the log odds of having attended a public meeting with a House member or senator by 1.92 across the trait's full range (2006 CES). No study of officials who host town halls was found, so the attendee coefficient stands in for the host (the same extraversion pull toward being in the room). Carried to the thirds of people leaning most and least toward holding one, that is a log odds gap of 1.088 (odds ratio 2.97). Weight found by crossing the real cases the decision weighed (the host's reasons without personality, cause plus effort, from played years of drawn places with the label trait-wiring) with every adult's lean toward holding one, at weights 0 to 3, net of the gap at weight 0, and solving for 0.837: 0.61. Rescaled Oct 24 by the trait's own standard deviation from the paper's Table 1 (0.26 of its full range, against the 0.2 first assumed), so the target grew by 1.3 to 1.088. Refitted Oct 26 on the cases weighed in six played election windows (Sula, Montana; Beulah, Mississippi; Cushing, Iowa; Kitzmiller, Maryland; Stratton, Colorado; Brook Forest, Colorado; 38 to 152 cases each, every adult's lean), because at 0.79 every town's net log odds sat from 3.2 to 4.7, three to four times the target: the geometric mean of the six is 1.095 at 0.35 (towns 0.64 to 1.60), against 0.79 at 0.3 and 1.37 at 0.4.

spread.citation: Weight scales with the coefficient: the study's 95% interval for the extraversion coefficient is 1.195 to 2.645.

traitWeightCampaignsPartyFirmness.citation: Mondak, Hibbing, Canache, Seligson and Anderson (2010), Personality and Civic Engagement, American Political Science Review 104(1), Table 2, worked for a party or candidate, openness logit 2.02 (interval 0.57 to 3.47), as the proxy for holding a party's line (no study of party firmness by personality was found): target odds ratio 2.63 between thirds (2.41 before the rescale below). Firmness is a share around one half, so the weight is the one at which the odds of a firm tie between the top and bottom third of lean differ by 2.37 across the adults of Newfane VT (seed c1). Rescaled Oct 24 by the trait's own standard deviation from the paper's Table 1 (0.22 of its full range, against the 0.2 first assumed), so the target grows by 1.1 and the weight is scaled by the same 1.1: 0.44 became 0.484. Not found again by measure: the fit above cannot be repeated on today's code, where on the adults of Newfane VT (seed c1) at the opening the odds of a firm tie between the thirds differ by only 1.35 at 0.44 and never pass about 1.5 at any weight (firmness is held between 0 and 1).

spread.citation: Scaled linearly from the study's reported interval (or half to one and a half times where none is reported) to the weight.

traitWeightEstatesWill.citation: The trait weight of the estates.will decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightEstatesTrust.citation: The trait weight of the estates.trust decision. Starts at the general traitWeight (1); calibrated against its row in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

spread.reason: Set from the researched effect size of this decision once calibrated; until then the general weight's spread, 0.2 to 1.0.

traitWeightLegislatureAttendSitting.citation: The trait weight of the legislature.attend-sitting decision. Salgado (2002), 'The Big Five personality dimensions and counterproductive behaviors' (Int. J. Selection and Assessment 10), found no Big Five trait significantly predicting absenteeism, so the trait share is the smallest in this family: half the 0.2 of legislature.member-position, which is r = .1 against r = .2. scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts could not fit it, because with a seat, session and close-vote duty most gated sittings are attended whatever the temperament (a miss rate near 1 percent leaves no gap between the thirds), so the weight is set by that ratio and checked by how many sittings personality turns (about 8 of 100 gated sittings, down from 96 of 100 when personality was the only reason). Pooled over 1,916 sittings in two played years after officials carry every trait (Pomona, New Jersey, seed 7628f7fcf9e0; seed f9a9cd8421fe), the choice saturates: a member's case for attending barely varies, so even a small trait term decides it (odds ratio 6,551 at weight 1), and no weight reaches the target; it stays the smallest in the family.
traitWeightLegislatureAttendSitting.estimatedFrom: traitWeightLegislatureMemberPosition (0.2) halved for r = .1; Salgado 2002 found no significant Big Five predictor of absenteeism.

spread.citation: Weight at r = .1 and r = .3 of the single-occasion range (half and one and a half times the r = .2 weight).

traitWeightLegislaturePoisonPill.citation: The trait weight of the legislature.poison-pill decision. One call in the audit year, so no calibration sample; this carries the weight calibrated for legislature.member-position (same legislators, same record), with the default target (the default personality-behavior study scaled for a single occasion to r = .2).

spread.citation: Weight at r = .1 and r = .3 of the single-occasion range (half and one and a half times the r = .2 weight).

traitWeightOfficeDayStateAttend.citation: The trait weight of the office-day-state.attend decision. Carries the weight of legislature.attend-sitting (the same behavior, absenteeism, where Salgado 2002 found no significant Big Five predictor). scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts cannot fit it on the audit year's 315 calls: every member attended, because the attendance duty of 0.6 outweighs any temperament (lean tops out near 0.6 and the weight is a fraction of that), which matches real attendance above 90 percent.

spread.citation: Weight at r = .1 and r = .3 of the single-occasion range (half and one and a half times the r = .2 weight).

traitWeightOfficeDayStateLeaderRequest.citation: The trait weight of the office-day-state.leader-request decision, found with scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts on two played years pooled, after officials carry a level on every trait (pool item officials-carry-every-trait): Pomona, New Jersey (key 3460030, seed 7628f7fcf9e0) and the place drawn from seed f9a9cd8421fe (key 2684360): 1.7 gives an odds ratio of 2.49 between the thirds of 106 requests, against the target of 2.24. Each place alone saturates (fits of 1.65 and 2.15 that cannot reach the target). It was 0.2, the single-occasion default, before officials carried every trait.

spread.citation: The two places' own best weights.

traitWeightAppointmentsWeigh.citation: The trait weight of the appointments.weigh decision: how far an appointer's traits tilt loyalty against merit when weighing a nominee (a lean of 1 counts loyalty 1.5 and merit 0.5). Replaces the appointmentLoyaltyMeritSwing of 0.5 (patronage studies: Lewis 2008). Not a two-way outcome, so scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts cannot fit it.

spread.citation: Weight at r = .1 and r = .3 of the single-occasion range (half and one and a half times the r = .2 weight).

traitWeightJobsRaiseForOpening.citation: The trait weight of the jobs.raise-for-opening decision: how far an owner's open-handedness scales what they add to an unfilled seat's pay (the share added is one half of 1 plus the weight times the lean, so a lean of 1 adds the full cost the seat has run up and a lean of -1 adds nothing). Not a two-way outcome, so scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts cannot fit it; unchanged from the site's earlier one-half-of-1-plus-lean.

spread.citation: Weight at r = .1 and r = .3 of the single-occasion range (half and one and a half times the r = .2 weight).

traitWeightRelationshipsWarmTo.citation: Jokela, Alvergne, Pollet & Lummaa 2011, 'Reproductive behavior and personality traits of the Five Factor Model', European Journal of Personality, Table 2: odds of a first marriage 1.35 per SD of extraversion, the nearest sourced measure of how readily warm, outgoing people form close ties (Selfhout et al. 2010 report the direction for friendship selection without an extractable size). The weight is ln(1.35) over the person-level standard deviation of the warm-to lean, 0.262, measured over 1,813 full people of a drawn place (buildBenchWorld seed sd1), so a pair one standard deviation warmer builds closeness 1.35 times as fast.

spread.citation: Men 1.53 and women 1.22 per SD (same table) give ln(1.22)/0.262 to ln(1.53)/0.262; the low end also covers a lean spread up to 0.31.

traitWeightRelationshipsFallOut.citation: Roberts, Kuncel, Shiner, Caspi & Goldberg 2007, 'The power of personality', Perspectives on Psychological Science: agreeableness and divorce, r = -0.18, the nearest sourced measure of how much a quarrel costs a tie between people who hold on to it (Jensen-Campbell & Graziano 2001 give the direction for conflict). Converted to 1.39 times the loss per SD (logit pi/sqrt(3) times r/sqrt(1-r^2)) and divided by the person-level standard deviation of the fall-out lean, 0.326, measured over 1,813 full people of a drawn place (buildBenchWorld seed sd1).

spread.citation: The conscientiousness (r = -0.13) and neuroticism (r = 0.17) divorce correlations in the same paper bound the size from 1.27 to 1.39 per SD; the high end allows a smaller lean spread.

relationshipsWarmToLeanCenter.citation: The mean warm-to lean of 1,813 full people in a drawn place (buildBenchWorld seed sd1), subtracted so the average pair keeps the closeness model's hours (Hall 2019).

spread.citation: The mean moves with each place's age and sex mix; checked against the standard deviation 0.262 over the root of the people counted.

relationshipsFallOutLeanCenter.citation: The mean fall-out lean of 1,813 full people in a drawn place (buildBenchWorld seed sd1), subtracted so the average quarrel costs the hours the engine that wrote it set.

spread.citation: The mean moves with each place's age and sex mix; checked against the standard deviation 0.326.

srrsFiredAtWork.citation: Holmes TH, Rahe RH. The Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Journal of Psychosomatic Research 11(2):213-218, 1967, Table 3 life change units. Item 8, fired at work: 47 units.

srrsForeclosure.citation: Holmes TH, Rahe RH. The Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Journal of Psychosomatic Research 11(2):213-218, 1967, Table 3 life change units. Item 22, foreclosure of mortgage or loan: 30 units (stands for losing a home to eviction).

srrsChangeInFinancialState.citation: Holmes TH, Rahe RH. The Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Journal of Psychosomatic Research 11(2):213-218, 1967, Table 3 life change units. Item 16, change in financial state: 38 units (stands for falling behind on a loan payment).

healthConscientiousnessLogHazardPerLevel.citation: Kern, M. L., & Friedman, H. S. (2008), Do conscientious individuals live longer? A quantitative review, Health Psychology 27(5), 505-512: r = .11 (95% CI .05-.17) with longevity. Converted to a hazard slope: r times a lifespan SD of 15 years is 1.65 years per trait SD; adult mortality doubles about every 8 years (Gompertz slope 0.087 per year), so a 1.65-year shift is a log hazard of -0.144 per SD; the opening levels have SD 1.095, giving -0.128 per level.
healthConscientiousnessLogHazardPerLevel.estimatedFrom: Lifespan SD and the Gompertz slope are round figures, not drawn from the life table.

spread.citation: Kern and Friedman 2008 confidence interval r .05 to .17, same conversion.

healthDrugUseLogOddsPerLevel.citation: Bogg, T., & Roberts, B. W. (2004), Conscientiousness and health-related behaviors: A meta-analysis of the leading behavioral contributors to mortality, Psychological Bulletin 130(6), 887-919: conscientiousness with drug use r = -.28, the largest domain. Point-biserial to logit slope per SD is r over sqrt(q(1-q)) with q = 0.15 holding the condition (pack prevalence 8.5-27%), -0.784 per SD, divided by the level SD 1.095.
healthDrugUseLogOddsPerLevel.estimatedFrom: One holding share for all ages; the slope per SD would be steeper where fewer hold it.

spread.citation: Bogg and Roberts 2004: other behavioral domains -.12 to -.25, drug use -.28.

healthYouthCannabisPastMonthShare.citation: SAMHSA, 2023-2024 National Surveys on Drug Use and Health, State Estimates, Table 3 (Marijuana Use in the Past Month), Total U.S., 12-17: 6.01 percent (95% CI 5.59-6.47), https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56957/2024-nsduh-sae-tables-percent-csvs/2024-nsduh-sae-tables-percent.pdf, read October 29, 2026. The 2023 Annual National Report agrees: "adolescents aged 12 to 17 (6.0 percent or 1.6 million people)" used marijuana in the past month (https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt47095/National%20Report/National%20Report/2023-nsduh-annual-national.htm).
healthYouthCannabisPastMonthShare.estimatedFrom: The national share of 12- to 17-year-olds who used marijuana in the past month stands in for each place's own share, which the same table gives by state; the state's law on sales moves it through the outcome web's link (cannabis-sales-to-youth-use), not through this number.

spread.citation: SAMHSA NSDUH 2023-2024 Table 3, 12-17 past-month use by state: lowest Hawaii 3.65 percent, highest Maine 9.87 percent.

healthTobaccoLogOddsPerLevel.citation: Bogg, T., & Roberts, B. W. (2004), Conscientiousness and health-related behaviors: A meta-analysis of the leading behavioral contributors to mortality, Psychological Bulletin 130(6), 887-919: conscientiousness with the other health behaviors r = -.12 to -.25 (midpoint -.185 for tobacco). Logit slope per SD is r over sqrt(q(1-q)) with q = 0.116 adult current smokers (CDC 2022), -0.578 per SD, divided by the level SD 1.095. Applied to the chronic lung disease condition smoking drives.
healthTobaccoLogOddsPerLevel.estimatedFrom: The tobacco domain value is not separately retrieved; the midpoint of the reported range stands in.

spread.citation: Bogg and Roberts 2004 range r -.12 to -.25.

traitChangeEventShift.citation: Direction: emotional stability falls after adverse life events (Specht, J. (2017), Personality development across the lifespan, and Specht, Egloff, & Schmukle (2011), Stability and change of personality across the life course: The impact of age and major life events on mean-level and rank-order stability of the Big Five, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 101(4), 862-882). Size: one event moves the hidden standard score of each emotional-stability trait by 0.1 of a standard deviation, in the range the event studies report as small; the per-event coefficients in the papers were not retrieved.
traitChangeEventShift.estimatedFrom: The size is a round figure inside "small"; only the direction is from the sources.

spread.citation: Small effects in the life-event personality literature; not retrieved per event.

traitWeightViewsPersuasion.citation: Hibbing, Ritchie and Anderson 2011 (rows views.persuasion in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json): openness raises the log odds of being moved toward a discussion partner's view by 0.66 across the trait's range (trait sd 0.22), an odds ratio of 1.37 between the thirds. A move is a size, so the weight is set so the most yielding third's mean move over the least yielding third's, net of the same ratio without the trait term, is 1.37. Fitted on the audit's kept samples (each the level with and without the trait term) in two played years, buildBenchWorld, every module: Lookeba, Oklahoma (place key 4044000, seed f20e6549007c, December 3, 2025 to December 3, 2026, around its November 2026 race) and Jagual, Puerto Rico (7237166, seed d29d296abf1f, January 20, 2025 to January 20, 2026). At 0.3 the ratio is 1.36 in Lookeba and 1.35 in Jagual.

spread.citation: The fit's neighbors: 0.2 gives 1.22 to 1.23 and 0.4 gives 1.49 to 1.51.

traitWeightViewsTrust.citation: Sindermann, Schmitt and others 2021 (row views.trust in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json): agreeableness correlates 0.20 with the Interpersonal Trust Scale among German adults (neuroticism -0.17; Thielmann et al. 2020 give 0.09 to 0.11 for trust-game sending). The weight is set so the hearer's lean correlates 0.20 with how far they trust a speaker. Fitted on the audit's kept samples (each the level with and without the trait term) in two played years, buildBenchWorld, every module: Lookeba, Oklahoma (place key 4044000, seed f20e6549007c, December 3, 2025 to December 3, 2026, around its November 2026 race) and Jagual, Puerto Rico (7237166, seed d29d296abf1f, January 20, 2025 to January 20, 2026). Pooled over 29,256 trust readings, 0.25 gives 0.203 (0.119 in Lookeba, 0.302 in Jagual: how far near ties already track the lean differs by town).

spread.citation: The pooled fit's neighbors: 0.15 gives 0.141 and 0.35 gives 0.256.

workAbsenceIllnessWeight.citation: BLS Current Population Survey 2023, Table 46: full-time wage and salary workers lose 1.7% of scheduled hours to absence (lost worktime rate), illness or injury being about two thirds of absences (2.2 of a 3.2% absence rate, data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json). The weight on a person's own care need (src/core2/modules/health.ts careNeedOf, 0 to 1) is set so missed shifts come to that share: in Ely, Nevada (key 3223500, seed 7ae8589566f5, 45 played days, 3,782 shift weighings) weights 0.2, 0.5 and 1.5 gave 1.1%, 3.7% and 11.1% of shifts missed; 0.3 sits at the 1.7% target.

spread.unit: score per unit of care need
spread.citation: The 1.2% to 2.5% lost-worktime band of data/research/stopgaps-oct19/A-people-behavior-1.json.

budgetHearingLeadDays.citation: How long before the fiscal year the body holds its public hearing on the executive's budget: the Government Finance Officers Association's budget-process practice and the truth-in-budgeting hearing laws many states set put the hearing two to six weeks before adoption, after the proposal is in the body's hands.
budgetHearingLeadDays.estimatedFrom: Common statutory and charter hearing lead times; no count of every place's charter exists.

spread.citation: Two to six weeks before adoption (GFOA budget-process practice).

coarsePlaceOldestWorkingAge.citation: The oldest age a worker met in another place is drawn up to when the last Census age row (75 and over) has no upper bound; the ACS reports employed people 75 and over as one row, and few are past 80.

spread.citation: Chosen range: the oldest working ages in the ACS 75-and-over row, which has no upper bound; checked by whether the drawn ages stay plausible, not measured.

coarsePlaceWagePercentile.citation: Where in their occupation's published wage distribution a worker met in another place is paid: the median, since the place's counts show how many hold each job and its wage table shows the middle, not who earns more; the player's own town spreads pay by tenure instead.

spread.citation: The BLS OEWS wage tables publish the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles; the player's own town starts a worker at the 25th and moves toward the 75th with tenure, so the median sits inside that range.

schoolStandingAttendanceWeight.citation: The unit of the standing that orders students within an income fifth: a student's share of school days attended counts at weight 1, and the study traits at schoolStandingTraitWeight against it. The standing only ranks who in a fifth passes or graduates (the count comes from the place's base, the web's factor and the income gradient), so only the ratio of the two weights matters and this one is the reference.

spread.citation: Fixed as the reference: scaling both weights together leaves every student's rank, and so every result record, unchanged.

schoolStandingTraitWeight.citation: Weight of the student's study traits (studious, voluntary effort) in that standing, against attendance at 1: the ratio of the two predictors' correlations with grades. Conscientiousness correlates with academic performance at rho .21 in secondary school, .28 in primary and .23 in tertiary (Poropat 2009, Psychological Bulletin 135(2), Table 2); class attendance correlates with class grades at rho .44 and with GPA at .41 (Credé, Roch and Kieszczynka 2010, Review of Educational Research 80(2)). Ordering only, never the level, which is the researched base.
schoolStandingTraitWeight.estimatedFrom: Poropat's secondary-school conscientiousness correlation (.21) over Credé, Roch and Kieszczynka's attendance and class-grade correlation (.44) is 0.48, rounded to 0.5. Both are correlations with grades, not a model with both predictors, so the ratio is an estimate of their relative pull.

spread.citation: From secondary conscientiousness over attendance and class grades (.21/.44 = 0.48) or GPA (.21/.41 = 0.51), to primary over class grades (.28/.44 = 0.64).

budgetWorldLineSpreadShare.citation: How far a world's budget line sits from the published one, as a share of it: about a year's change in a state or local government's line (Census Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances, fiscal 2021 to 2022, functions moved 2% to 10%) and the federal receipts and outlays' year-to-year change (Monthly Treasury Statement, fiscal 2024 to 2025).
budgetWorldLineSpreadShare.estimatedFrom: Owner, Oct 27: real data calibrates, every start differs (realistic, not real). officialSavingsSpreadSigma.citation: How widely one seated official's savings sit around the median a family at their pay keeps (the log-normal standard deviation; the median itself is unchanged). Officials at one pay were all given the same balance, so a body of 190 legislators had no one with a thin cushion and the bribe engine's money pressure never moved between them. The Survey of Consumer Finances 2022 puts the median transaction-account balance of holders at $8,000 and the mean at $62,500 (Federal Reserve Bulletin, Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022, table of holdings by asset type), which a log-normal reads as a standard deviation of 2.0 across all families. An official at one pay holds a narrower range than all families, but the mean is carried by a few large balances while the lower tail, which the bribe engine reads, is wide, so the all-family figure is used and its lower half is the spread.

businessWorldCountSpreadShare.citation: How far a world's count of a kind of business in a town sits from the published expectation (County Business Patterns 2023 establishments per resident times the town's population): the county's count of a kind moves 2% to 10% a year, and a town's share of it is an estimate by population.

spread.citation: Checked against BLS CPS labor force participation by age: participation falls steeply after 64; the opening's employment rate by age (opening-employment.ts) is the check.

townJobsFullTimeMaximumWeeklyHours.citation: Ported unchanged from the old engine's town-employment-v1 opening fill (src/core2/opening-town-jobs.ts), where it was a GAME ASSUMPTION; the upper end of a full-time role's expected weekly hours; the lower end is fullTimeWeeklyHours.

spread.citation: Checked against BLS CPS Table 19: people usually working full time averaged about 42 to 43 hours a week at work.

townJobsPartTimeMinimumWeeklyHours.citation: Ported unchanged from the old engine's town-employment-v1 opening fill (src/core2/opening-town-jobs.ts), where it was a GAME ASSUMPTION; the lower end of a part-time role's expected weekly hours.

speechCraftHalfAddresses.citation: How many recorded addresses a speaker has given when their craft is half of what it can become (craft = addresses / (addresses + this)). No source measures the learning curve of public speaking in addresses given; set so a speaker who gives an address about once a month is at half craft after a year.

spread.citation: Chosen range; no study sets how many addresses it takes a speaker to master a device. Checked by a new speaker's first addresses being plain and a speaker of many addresses using the devices, not measured.

speechDeviceQuotationDifficulty.citation: Where on the craft scale (0 to 1) a speaker first has the quotation device in hand: a speaker whose craft is at or above it may use the device where the setting admits it. Ordered from easiest (quoting) to hardest (calling back to an earlier address); the order, not the numbers, is the design.

employmentCellPriorCount.citation: The Jeffreys prior for a binomial share, Beta(1/2, 1/2): a share read from x of n people is estimated as (x + 1/2) / (n + 1), which stays strictly between none and all for any sample. Brown, Cai and DasGupta (2001), Interval Estimation for a Binomial Proportion, Statistical Science 16(2): 101-133, recommend the Jeffreys interval for small samples; its center is this estimate. Read by publishedResidentEmploymentRate for the ACS county age cells (B23001 counts of a few dozen in small counties).

worldSmallDollarVolumeSpreadShare.citation: How far a world's small-dollar lending volume (the households that borrow from the town's payday or high-cost installment lender, and so the cash the lender lends) sits from the sourced national figure for a place, as a share of it. National household use fell from 1.5 percent in 2019 to 1.1 percent in 2021 (FDIC National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households, Table 5.2), a change of about a quarter.
